Value proposition: T1: reliable, serviced self-service laundry that maximises operator uptime and ROI, sold as machines plus service. T2: a compact commercial-grade machine with longer life and faster cycles, sold direct. Neither is supported by independent evidence yet.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run test X1 (proposed: about EUR 20,000 over 12 weeks, two arms). Arm A counts signed operator pilot letters from about 15 operators. Arm B measures deposit conversion on a compact-machine landing page. Decide by the proposed decision rule.. Uncertainty: High. All company-side support for T1 is EPG's own marketing. No independent study on operator purchase criteria was found. The only independent source is a 2015 German release on appliance replacement, not commercial-grade demand or EPG. EPG segment revenue, margins, channel contracts and brand licences were not found, and may be non-public. My challenge on T1 returned only company pages, so it was not a real test. Thresholds and sample sizes are my estimates.. Would change if: Test X1 Arm A yields fewer than 2 of 15 operator letters, which weakens T1 and points to no expansion; Arm B reaches at least 1% deposit conversion with at least 60% finishing installation, which favours T2; Independent evidence shows operators buy mainly on price, undermining T1's value capture; EPG disclosures show an existing consumer channel, or brand or contract conflicts that block direct sales; Margin data shows a consumer channel cannot cover the EUR 20,000 test plus scale-up costs. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

case.question: Should RATIONAL develop a differentiated proposition for home cooks, building on its commercial combi-steamer technology, or stay with professional kitchens? What evidence would justify either choice?
case.source_limits: Evidence is limited to the case dossier: each source shows everything the dossier holds for it, often a short excerpt, not the whole original. Results marked simulated are what-if evidence, not real observations.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 32 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 72 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.

Subsequent products included the Anova Precision Cooker Nano and the Anova Precision Oven, a countertop combi oven that supported both steam and convection cooking methods and could be used either alongside other Precision Cooker products or by itself.
These countertop appliances have the same characteristic changes as the full-size household appliances, except that they are smaller, and cost significantly less than a full-size oven.
Germany: RATIONAL AG , Gaggenau Hausgeräte , PALUX, Convotherm, MKN, ELOMA, Miele , AEG (part of Electrolux), Bosch.
We concentrate on what we do best: the preparation of hot food in professional kitchens.

The customer base ranges from restaurants and hotels, company canteens, hospitals, schools, universities, the military, prisons and retirement homes to fast-food restaurants, party services, supermarkets, bakeries and snack bars, butchers, petrol stations and delivery services, including so-called ghost kitchens.
According to company estimates, the global market potential for combi-steamers is 4.8 million customers, around 75% of whom still use traditional cooking appliances.
From 1978 onwards, the company concentrated solely on combi steamers and discontinued all other product lines.

events.text: Objective: Decide whether RATIONAL AG should build a differentiated proposition for home cooks using its commercial combi-steamer technology, or keep its focus on professional kitchens, and identify what evidence would justify either choice. Also establish how far RATIONAL already reaches individual buyers.. Constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only; no company contact or insider knowledge; Company has not asked this question; nothing here describes its intentions; Financial data partly public; must state what could not be found or reconciled; Test budget 20000 EUR and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions, not company figures; Search budget of 8 searches (7 remaining after read_brief); challenge uses one search; Numbers presented as observed must come from sources read; proposed numbers must be labelled. Alternatives: No expansion: stay with professional commercial kitchens and existing channels, including hospitality expansion in existing regions; Premium consumer line: a home-sized combi-steamer with product redesign, sold through existing appliance retail channels; Accessory or cooking-method route: sell recipes, software or steam accessories compatible with professional units, without new hardware; Channel route: sell existing units or prosumer models to individual buyers through online direct or partner retail, without redesign; Adjacent customer group: target small food businesses, catering or prosumers (serious home cooks with commercial-style needs) rather than mainstream home cooks; Licensing or partnership: license steam-cooking technology to an existing home-appliance maker, keeping the professional line intact.
Searched for "RATIONAL combi steamer home consumer"; found rational-combi-makers, rational-ir-potential, rational-wiki-1978.
Searched for "RATIONAL individual buyers home kitchen sales"; found rational-ir-customers, rational-focus-quote, rational-ir-figures.

T1: Home cooks will pay a premium for a compact combi-steamer if it is marketed as a health and time-saving appliance, so a maker that already owns steam-cooking know-how could earn premium margins on a home-sized unit. Who benefits: The manufacturer (premium margin on a new unit) and home cooks seeking healthier, faster cooking.. Why behaviour changes: Home cooks adopt steam and combi cooking once it is framed as a healthy, low-effort alternative to conventional ovens, and once a credible brand reduces the perceived risk of a high-priced appliance.. How value is captured: Direct or premium retail sale of a redesigned home unit, priced above conventional built-in ovens, with accessories and recipes as recurring revenue.. Assumptions: Home cooks have unmet demand for steam cooking that current built-in ovens do not satisfy; Consumers accept a price premium over conventional built-in ovens; A professional brand transfers credibility to the home category; Kitchen space and installation are not a binding barrier. Predictions: A home-sized prototype sold at a premium price should get pre-orders from a measurable share of target households in a landing-page or pre-order test; Buyers should cite health and time savings more than professional brand as their reason to buy; Conversion should fall sharply when price rises above the built-in oven range.

T2: Home demand for combi-steamers is limited by kitchen installation and space, so any home value flows to built-in appliance makers who already control fitting, retail and service, and a steam-technology owner captures value mainly by licensing rather than selling directly. Who benefits: Incumbent built-in appliance brands and fitters who control installation and retail; RATIONAL only if it licenses its technology.. Why behaviour changes: Home cooks buy when a built-in unit fits their existing kitchen and is sold and installed through a trusted channel, so the buying decision depends on the installation pathway more than on the cooking technology.. How value is captured: Licence fees or component supply to an established built-in appliance maker, with RATIONAL keeping its professional brand and channel.. Assumptions: Built-in kitchen installation is the main purchase route for ovens in target markets; Appliance makers would pay for steam technology they cannot develop themselves; Direct-to-consumer sales of a large unit would struggle without installation service. Predictions: Home buyers who view a unit in a showroom should ask about installation and fitting before price; A direct online-only home offer should see lower conversion than the same product sold through a built-in appliance retailer; Licensing interest should come from built-in makers, not from direct consumer enquiries.

T1 neutral, from rational-focus-quote (company_assertion): "We concentrate on what we do best: the preparation of hot food in professional kitchens.". Does not show: It is a company statement of strategic focus, reported by a third-party newsletter, not a market measurement. It says nothing about whether home cooks would pay a premium, and it does not show that RATIONAL has tested or rejected a home product..

T2 supports, from rational-combi-makers (market_fact): "Germany: RATIONAL AG , Gaggenau Hausgeräte , PALUX, Convotherm, MKN, ELOMA, Miele , AEG (part of Electrolux), Bosch.". Does not show: This is a list of Germany-listed combi-steamer makers. It does not say which of them sell home units, how those units are installed or sold, or whether installation is the binding barrier. It supports only the premise that built-in appliance makers already occupy the category..
Looked for evidence against T2: "home combi steamer sold direct online without installation consumer demand"; found rational-combi-countertop, rational-combi-differences, rational-combi-history.

T2 contradicts, from rational-combi-countertop (market_fact): "These countertop appliances have the same characteristic changes as the full-size household appliances, except that they are smaller, and cost significantly less than a full-size oven.". Does not show: This is a general encyclopedia description. It does not say which brands sell countertop units, in which countries, at what volumes, or whether they sell direct without installation. It weakens the claim that installation is the binding barrier, but does not show that home demand for these units is strong or that RATIONAL would capture value from them..

Test "Home steam-unit pre-order and route test" between T1; T2. Method: Two landing pages for a concept home steam unit, each with a pre-order or waitlist button. Arm A is a direct online pre-order at a premium price with health and time framing. Arm B is a built-in unit offer that asks for installer and retailer preference before price. Traffic comes from paid social and search targeted at home cooks in Germany. Pre-order is refundable, and no product is shipped.. Sample: Proposed: about 6,000 unique visitors per arm over 4 weeks, drawn from paid traffic in Germany only.. Measure: Pre-order or waitlist conversion rate per arm; share of Arm B visitors who choose an installation option before price; stated reason for purchase from a short post-click question.. Predictions: T1: Arm A converts at a meaningful rate, at least 2 to 3 percent of visitors, with health and time savings cited more than brand; conversion falls sharply when the premium price is shown.; T2: Arm B converts better than Arm A, and visitors ask about installation and fitting before price; direct online conversion is low.. Decision rule: Proposed: favour T1 only if Arm A pre-order conversion is at least 2 percent and Arm A exceeds Arm B by at least 1 percentage point. Favour T2 if Arm B exceeds Arm A by at least 1 percentage point and installation questions dominate. If both are below 0.5 percent, reject the home-product route for now.. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.
Looked for evidence against T1: "home combi steamer consumer willingness to pay premium health cooking"; found rational-ir-potential, rational-anova-oven, rational-combi-countertop.

T1 supports, from rational-anova-oven (market_fact): "Subsequent products included the Anova Precision Cooker Nano and the Anova Precision Oven, a countertop combi oven that supported both steam and convection cooking methods and could be used either alongside other Precision Cooker products or by itself.". Does not show: It shows that a consumer-brand countertop combi oven exists in one country. It does not show sales volumes, price premium, why buyers chose it, health or time framing, or whether a professional steam-tech owner would earn margin on a home unit..

Favours T1: Stay with professional kitchens as the core business. Do not redesign for home cooks yet. Run the proposed pre-order test (X1, not yet run) before deciding. T1 is favoured only as the hypothesis the test can falsify: sources show consumer countertop steam-combi products exist (Anova, and countertop units in general), but none I read measures home demand, premium willingness to pay or RATIONAL's capture of value. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: unlikely.

T2 kept: SYN-RATIONAL-UPDATE is SIMULATED and is not evidence. Hypothetically, if real, a 32 versus 72 reservation split would run against the T2 prediction that a bundled installer route would win; the purchaser-arranged offer did better. That would weaken T2's specific claim about coordinated installation. It does not touch the wider point that installation or space may limit home sales. T2 is kept, not revised, because I cannot use a simulated result to change my belief, and the existing evidence already weakens T2 through the countertop unit description. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-RATIONAL-UPDATE.

Recommendation: Do not build a home-cooks line now. Keep the core on professional kitchens. Before any redesign, run the proposed pre-order test (X1, not yet run, about 15,000 EUR over 6 weeks, a proposed design). Treat the home-cooks question as open until that test reports. Target customer: Not yet chosen. Candidate: affluent home cooks who already buy countertop steam or combi appliances. Not a decided segment.. Value proposition: Untested. Hypothesis (T1): a compact steam-combi that buyers see as a healthy, time-saving appliance, priced above conventional built-in ovens. No source I read measures this.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the X1 pre-order test with two arms, one direct online at a premium price and one with a built-in installer route, and apply the decision rule: favour home only if direct pre-order conversion is at least 2 percent and beats the installer arm by at least 1 point; reject for now if both are below 0.5 percent.. Uncertainty: Large. I found no source giving RATIONAL's home sales, home product plans or consumer revenue, and I did not read its financial reports, so I cannot say how far it already reaches individual buyers beyond what the sources state. The 4.8 million market figure is a company estimate and covers professional customers. Sources show countertop and consumer combi units exist (Anova; countertop units in general) but give no volumes, prices or buyer reasons. The installation barrier (T2) is weakened but not tested.. Would change if: X1 shows direct pre-order conversion at or above 2 percent with health and time framing cited over brand; X1 shows the installer arm clearly beating direct online, which would favour a licensing or built-in partner route; A verified source shows RATIONAL already sells to individual buyers in volume, which would change the baseline; A source shows consumer combi appliances failing on price or returns, which would weaken T1; Financial reports show professional growth slowing enough to make a new customer group worth the test cost. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: unlikely.

case.question: Should Electrolux Professional Group develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing professional laundry offering? What evidence would justify that investment?
case.source_limits: Evidence is limited to the case dossier: each source shows everything the dossier holds for it, often a short excerpt, not the whole original. Results marked simulated are what-if evidence, not real observations.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 household washing-machine buyers eligible for the same professional-derived washer offer were assigned equally to two descriptions. Both descriptions showed the same machine, brand, price, warranty, availability, service terms and verified specifications. One emphasized durability and repairability; the other emphasized washing performance and the upfront price. No discount or extra service was added. The outcome was a paid, refundable purchase reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned buyers per arm. There were 72 reservations in the durability-and-repairability description arm and 32 in the performance-and-price description arm. This tests the incremental effect of the description in this recruited population, not actual appliance lifetime, delivery capability, market size, profitability or sustained repurchase. A weaker result would not refute a different channel or product theory.

In addition, residential customers are increasingly demanding commercial-quality products for the home, and our machines represent a compelling fit for this select but growing segment of the residential market.
Consumer‑operated setups enable residents, guests or members to run their own laundry in multi‑family buildings, student housing, campsites, marinas, gyms or staff facilities.

Electrolux Professional provides integrated solutions designed for different formats – laundromats, bungalows and consumer‑operated – combining reliability, resource efficiency and serviceability to maximize uptime and ROI.
Our research has found that you don't have to pay a premium to make a sustainable choice. In fact, the cheapest Eco Buy dishwashers and washing machines cost less than £400.

events.text: Objective: Decide whether Electrolux Professional Group should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its professional laundry offering, and identify what evidence would justify that investment.. Constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only; no company contact or intentions assumed; Some financial and contractual detail may be non-public and must be flagged as not found; Test budget EUR 20000 and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions, not company figures; Search budget is limited; current consumer reach must be verified, not assumed. Alternatives: No expansion: stay professional-only and focus on existing commercial laundry and food-service customers; Product redesign: adapt professional machines into a smaller or simpler product for a specific consumer use case such as apartment or small-batch laundry; Different route to buyers: sell existing or adapted equipment to consumers through retail, online or subscription channels without a new product; Different customer group: serve an adjacent professional segment such as laundromats, small hospitality, care homes or rental operators; Partnership or licensing: license technology or brand to a consumer appliance maker and earn royalties without owning consumer channels; Aftermarket or service: offer consumer-facing parts, maintenance or consumables on the existing professional installed base without a new consumer product.
Searched for "Electrolux Professional consumer products home laundry"; found epro-consumer-operated, epro-selfservice-formats, epro-alliance-residential-segment.

T1: Some households will pay a premium for commercial-grade laundry machines because durability and repairability matter more to them than price or size. An EPG-branded residential line sold through appliance retail or online could capture that premium. Who benefits: Households that want long-life machines and EPG, which could earn premium margins on a product it already designs.. Why behaviour changes: Buyers who have seen or heard that professional machines last longer may switch from mid-range domestic models when they replace a machine, if the product is offered in a size and price they can accept.. How value is captured: A premium-priced residential SKU sold through retail or online channels, with margin above the domestic average, and possibly service plans.. Assumptions: A meaningful share of households replace machines on durability grounds rather than on features or price; The professional design can be shrunk or simplified for home installation without losing its durability advantage; EPG can reach home buyers through retail or online channels at acceptable cost. Predictions: Households shown a commercial-grade machine at a premium price will pre-order or join a waitlist at a measurable rate; Willingness to pay rises with stated durability and repairability, not with brand alone; Sales are concentrated in households with high-use or hard-water conditions.

T2: Residential demand for commercial-grade laundry does not reach individual households directly. It flows through landlords, property managers and operators who buy consumer-operated laundry for shared buildings, so EPG's value is captured by selling to those intermediaries rather than by building a consumer brand. Who benefits: Property owners and operators, who gain income from in-building laundry and need uptime and low service cost; EPG, which keeps its B2B channel and sells to the intermediary.. Why behaviour changes: Individual tenants or guests do not choose the machine. The landlord or operator chooses it on uptime, cost per cycle and serviceability, so consumer demand expresses itself as a building-level purchase.. How value is captured: Sell existing or lightly adapted self-service equipment to property and hospitality operators, with service contracts and consumables, rather than launching a consumer product.. Assumptions: Buyers of in-building laundry are landlords or operators, not households; Tenants value convenience of on-site laundry enough that landlords see a return; EPG's existing self-service range already fits multi-family and campsite formats. Predictions: Sales leads for consumer-operated units come from property managers and campsite operators rather than from households; Adoption rises with building size and falls with cost per cycle; Households who are offered a home machine directly show low interest compared with the building-level route.

T1 supports, from epro-alliance-residential-segment (company_assertion): "residential customers are increasingly demanding commercial-quality products for the home, and our machines represent a compelling fit for this select but growing segment of the residential market.". Does not show: This is a competitor's (Alliance Laundry Holdings) prospectus claim, not an EPG fact. It gives no segment size, sales figures, or price evidence, and it is North America focused. It cannot show that households would pay an EPG premium, that EPG could reach them, or that durability is their deciding factor. The IPO label says verified_observation, but the content is the company's own assertion about its market..

T2 supports, from epro-consumer-operated (company_assertion): "Consumer‑operated setups enable residents, guests or members to run their own laundry in multi‑family buildings, student housing, campsites, marinas, gyms or staff facilities.". Does not show: This is EPG's own product-page wording. It shows that EPG already sells consumer-operated laundry installed in shared buildings, which is a point in favour of T2. It does not show who makes the purchase decision (landlord, operator or tenant), how many units are sold, or whether any household would buy a machine directly. It is a claim about the product, not a measure of buyer behaviour..

Looked for evidence against T2: "individual households buy own commercial laundry machines directly; landlords reject in-building laundry"; found epro-consumer-operated, epro-alliance-residential-segment, epro-which-no-premium.

T1 contradicts, from epro-which-no-premium (customer_observation): "Our research has found that you don't have to pay a premium to make a sustainable choice. In fact, the cheapest Eco Buy dishwashers and washing machines cost less than £400.". Does not show: This is a 2020 UK consumer-testing result about sustainability ratings for mainstream domestic machines. It does not test commercial-grade durability, professional-equipment brands, or willingness to pay for longevity. It weakens only the assumption that a premium follows from an eco or quality label; it does not disprove T1..

Test "Building-operator versus household demand test" between T1; T2. Method: Run a two-arm landing-page and quote test in a single metro area. Arm A offers a residential commercial-grade machine directly to households at a stated premium price with a waitlist. Arm B offers a consumer-operated laundry installation to landlords, property managers and campsite operators, with a quote request and cost-per-cycle figures. Measure waitlist and quote-request conversion, and log who completes each form (household or building operator). Proposed, not run.. Sample: Proposed: about 3000 targeted ad impressions per arm to households and building operators in one metro area, plus 20 to 30 direct outreach contacts to property managers and campsite operators.. Measure: Qualified waitlist sign-ups per 1000 impressions for households (Arm A); qualified quote requests per 100 operator contacts (Arm B); share of Arm A sign-ups who state they own or rent the home and would decide alone.. Predictions: T1: Household waitlist conversion is comparable to or above the operator route, and households state durability as the main reason to sign up.; T2: Household waitlist conversion is low, while operator quote requests are clearly higher, and households who do sign up are mostly unable to decide alone.. Decision rule: Keep T1 as a live option only if household waitlist conversion is at least 1.5 times the operator quote-request rate per comparable unit of effort, with at least 30 qualified household sign-ups. Otherwise, favour T2 and move to an operator-focused next step. Thresholds are proposed, not drawn from any company data.. Cost: 12000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T2: Do not launch a consumer-branded residential product on the evidence so far. Treat the building-operator route as the more promising first step, using existing self-service equipment, and test household demand cheaply before committing to any product redesign. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: likely.

T1 kept: The only simulated result read so far is labelled SIMULATED and I am not citing it. No real evidence has changed T1: the competitor prospectus claim supports demand in principle but gives no sales figures, and the 2020 Which? result shows no premium for sustainability in mainstream machines, which weakens but does not disprove a premium for durability. T1 stays uncertain pending a real test. New claim: none. Evidence: epro-alliance-residential-segment; epro-which-no-premium.

T2 kept: No real evidence has changed T2. EPG's own product pages describe consumer-operated laundry in shared buildings, which fits T2, but they do not show who decides the purchase or how many units are sold. The simulated result SYN-EPRO-UPDATE concerns households and is not cited here, so it changes nothing. T2 remains the favoured theory, with the caveat that it has not been tested. New claim: none. Evidence: epro-consumer-operated; epro-selfservice-formats.

T1 kept: What-if only. If SYN-EPRO-UPDATE were real, it would mean that a durability-and-repairability description produced more purchase reservations than a performance-and-price description among recruited household buyers, which would favour T1 and suggest a premium for durability. Because it is labelled SIMULATED and is not real data, I have not applied that change. T1 stays uncertain, supported only by the competitor prospectus claim and weakened by the 2020 Which? result. The result is recorded here and is not cited as evidence. New claim: none. Evidence: epro-alliance-residential-segment; epro-which-no-premium.
The investigation stopped before a recommendation (repeated errors).

case.question: Should Aquaporin A/S develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing water-membrane offering? What evidence would justify that investment?
case.source_limits: Evidence is limited to the case dossier: each source shows everything the dossier holds for it, often a short excerpt, not the whole original. Results marked simulated are what-if evidence, not real observations.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. In this simulated warehouse test, a new label printer reduced packing errors slightly. Nothing about wearers or buyers was measured.

With only two cartridges and a replacement indicator on the machine, ONE is easy to install and use. The user friendliness continues, as ONE’s only maintenance requirement is cartridge replacement which can easily be done by oneself.

Signed an exclusive supply agreement with AquaShield, the global brand partner of Philips Water Solutions for supply of membrane to all Philips-branded purifiers in China, with a doubling of sales compared to 2022

Despite significant efforts through a period of time and as part of its strategic review in the second half of 2025, where multiple routes have been explored with the view to raise capital, enter into a strategic transaction, or a sale of part of or all of the Company's asset, the Company has not been successful in identifying investors or partners that can provide sufficient funding to continue the Company's commercialization and advancing its proprietary water technology platform. The Board of Directors does therefore not see a viable path forward to secure a sustainable financing solution as a going concern.

Turkey's leading technology company, Vestel, has launched a water purifier named Vestel Rafine PRO in cooperation with Aquaporin on its website and in selected stores across Turkey. The Aquaporin Inside® technology powers the Vestel Rafine PRO water purifier.

events.text: Objective: Decide whether Aquaporin should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for one specific use case, beyond its existing membrane offering, and identify what public evidence would justify that investment.. Constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only; the company has not asked and its intentions are unknown; Company financial data may be incomplete, so state what could not be found; Test budget of 20000 EUR and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions, not company figures; Search budget is limited, so first establish how far the company already reaches individual buyers; SIMULATED results are not real demand evidence. Alternatives: No expansion: keep selling membranes to OEM and industrial partners only; Product redesign: a consumer purifier or cartridge built around the existing membrane, under the company or a partner brand; Route change: license or supply the membrane to existing consumer purifier brands, business-to-business-to-consumer; Customer change: target one segment such as off-grid, travel, emergency or premium households in water-stressed regions; Adjacent use: a non-drinking application such as industrial wastewater or desalination pre-treatment, where the membrane supplier captures value; Partner-led pilot: co-develop with an existing consumer brand before committing own capital.
Searched for "Aquaporin consumer water purifier products"; found aqp-one-purifier-2021, aqp-philips-china-supply-2023, aqp-vestel-rafine-pro-2024.

T1: Consumers buy a home water purifier on the brand and its perceived water-safety promise, not on the membrane. Aquaporin captures value most reliably by supplying the membrane inside partner brands that own the retail relationship, so a self-branded consumer product would add cost and channel risk without a matching price premium. Who benefits: Aquaporin, as a component supplier with exclusive or high-volume partner contracts, and the partner brands that hold the consumer relationship.. Why behaviour changes: Buyers choose among purifier brands on design, distribution and trust in the appliance maker. An ingredient brand like 'Aquaporin Inside' only moves purchases if it is visible at point of sale and tied to a credible safety claim the partner can make.. How value is captured: Per-unit or per-cartridge membrane supply fees and exclusive supply agreements with brand partners, as with the Philips-branded supply in China and the Vestel product in Turkey.. Assumptions: Partner brands are willing to pay for an ingredient they can advertise; Retail and online channels for purifiers are controlled by appliance brands rather than by the membrane maker; Price premium from the membrane sits mainly with the partner brand. Predictions: Partner-branded units outsell any Aquaporin-branded unit in the same market; Partners ask for exclusivity and co-marketing rather than paying for a standalone Aquaporin brand; Retail listings show the Aquaporin name only in small print or as a sub-brand.

T2: In a specific use case where the buyer cannot rely on mains water or a standard filter, such as off-grid, travel or emergency use, a verifiable membrane performance claim becomes the purchase reason. A company that controls the membrane and sells a segment-specific product could then charge a premium and earn repeat cartridge revenue, which a generic partner brand would not capture. Who benefits: Households or travellers in the chosen segment, who gain a product that works without reliable infrastructure, and Aquaporin, which would keep the margin and the consumer data rather than ceding them to a partner brand.. Why behaviour changes: Buyers in that segment face a clear, costly failure risk and so pay for proof of performance. A specific, testable claim about contaminant removal beats generic 'premium filter' marketing when the alternative is untreated or unverified water.. How value is captured: A direct or segment-distributed product sold at a premium, with recurring replacement cartridges and possibly service contracts, plus the membrane supply margin.. Assumptions: A segment exists that is large enough and will pay more for verified performance; Aquaporin can reach that segment through distributors or direct channels without a large marketing budget; Certification or independent test data can be produced at acceptable cost. Predictions: Segment buyers ask for independent certification figures before purchase; Price-per-litre for cartridges in the segment is higher than in mainstream household purifiers; Partner brands in the segment avoid claims tied to a single contaminant spec.

T1 supports, from aqp-philips-china-supply-2023 (company_assertion): "Signed an exclusive supply agreement with AquaShield, the global brand partner of Philips Water Solutions for supply of membrane to all Philips-branded purifiers in China, with a doubling of sales compared to 2022". Does not show: Whether consumers chose the Philips units because of the Aquaporin membrane, or what share of the price premium Aquaporin receives. It is a company-written summary of a supply deal and its revenue effect..

T2 neutral, from aqp-one-purifier-2021 (company_assertion): "With only two cartridges and a replacement indicator on the machine, ONE is easy to install and use.". Does not show: Any specific segment such as off-grid, travel or emergency buyers, any verified performance claim, or any price premium. The press release sells a generic home purifier on ease of use across broad markets, which is the mainstream case T2 says is not differentiated..

Looked for evidence against T1: "Aquaporin partner dependence risk exclusivity margin own brand consumer sales"; found aqp-philips-china-supply-2023, aqp-strategic-review-failed, aqp-one-purifier-2021.
Searched for "Aquaporin insolvency 2026 asset sale buyer"; found aqp-strategic-review-failed, aqp-insolvency-2026, aqp-philips-china-supply-2023.

Declined to test: The company announced on 30 January 2026 that it has withdrawn its offering and resolved to initiate insolvency proceedings, after failing to find investors or partners to fund commercialisation as a going concern. A 20000 EUR, 12-week consumer test would be spent on a business that cannot fund the proposition it would test, and no public source shows a buyer, licensee or restart plan. Any further test would only be worth running for a party that could acquire the membrane platform, and that is a different question from the one asked. No further test is justified here.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition. Aquaporin has announced withdrawal of its offering and the initiation of insolvency proceedings, so there is no funded company to make the investment. If any party considers the membrane platform, the only evidence-backed route to consumers is supplying the membrane inside partner brands, which is what the company already tried in China and Turkey. A self-branded segment product (T2) is not supported by any source read. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: unlikely.

T1 kept: SYN-D is a SIMULATED warehouse test about label printers and packing errors. It measures nothing about buyers or wearers, so it does not bear on T1 and changes nothing. T1 stays as stated, resting on the real company claims and the insolvency announcement, which show partner supply in China and Turkey but no evidence that a self-branded product would earn a premium. New claim: none. Evidence: aqp-philips-china-supply-2023; aqp-vestel-rafine-pro-2024; aqp-strategic-review-failed.

T2 kept: Suppose SYN-D were real. It is a simulated warehouse test of label printers and packing errors, and it says nothing about buyers, wearers, segments or price. Even if it were real it would not bear on T2, so T2 is kept unchanged and remains unsupported by any source read. New claim: none. Evidence: aqp-one-purifier-2021.

T1 kept: Suppose SYN-D were real. It would be a warehouse test of label printers and packing errors, which measures nothing about buyers or wearers, so it would change nothing for T1. T1 stays kept on the real company claims and the insolvency announcement. SYN-D is recorded here only as a what-if and is excluded from all real evidence. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for Aquaporin. On 30 January 2026 the company announced it had withdrawn its offering and resolved to initiate insolvency proceedings, after failing to find investors or partners to fund commercialisation as a going concern. There is no funded company to make the investment. The only consumer route the public evidence supports is supplying the membrane inside partner brands, which the company had already done in China and Turkey. Any further work should be limited to an acquirer or licensee of the membrane platform, and that is a different question. Target customer: None for Aquaporin itself. Partner appliance brands that buy membrane supply are the only consumer-facing route the evidence supports. The off-grid or emergency segment in T2 is untested and has no supporting source.. Value proposition: Not applicable for Aquaporin as a standalone consumer brand. The membrane supply model (Philips-branded purifiers in China, Vestel Rafine PRO in Turkey) is the only one with public evidence, and it depends on a partner brand carrying the consumer relationship.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Check the insolvency filing and any sale or asset process with the Danish insolvency administrator and the company's announcements, to establish whether the membrane platform, patents or partner contracts are for sale. No consumer test is recommended.. Uncertainty: Financial data is incomplete: I found no balance sheet, cash runway, debt or insolvency-administrator statement, and no public information on partner contract terms, volumes or price premiums. The evidence is almost entirely company-written press releases, and the 2023 revenue growth figure is a company claim with no independent check. I could not establish whether any party is buying the platform. SYN-D was simulated and was excluded from all evidence.. Would change if: A named buyer, licensee or investor publicly takes over the membrane platform or the partner contracts; The insolvency administrator's filing shows the membrane technology or partner supply contracts are sold as a going concern; Independent data shows partner-branded purifiers sell at a price premium attributable to the membrane, which would support T1 further; Independent evidence shows a specific off-grid or emergency segment paying more for verified membrane performance, which would support T2. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: unlikely.

case.question: Should RATIONAL develop a differentiated proposition for home cooks, building on its commercial combi-steamer technology, or stay with professional kitchens? What evidence would justify either choice?
case.source_limits: Evidence is limited to the case dossier: each source shows everything the dossier holds for it, often a short excerpt, not the whole original. Results marked simulated are what-if evidence, not real observations.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 72 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 32 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.
On February 6, 2017, Anova was acquired by Electrolux , a home appliance company, for a total of US$250 million.
These countertop appliances have the same characteristic changes as the full-size household appliances, except that they are smaller, and cost significantly less than a full-size oven.
According to company estimates, the global market potential for combi-steamers is 4.8 million customers, around 75% of whom still use traditional cooking appliances.
Combi ovens (iCombi product line) generate approximately 90% of Rational's appliance sales, while about 10% comes from the iVario series and newly added iHexagon appliances.

events.text: Objective: Decide whether RATIONAL AG should build a differentiated proposition for home cooks using its commercial combi-steamer technology, or keep focusing on professional kitchens, and identify what evidence would justify either choice.. Constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only; no company contact or insider intentions; Search budget of 8 searches (7 left after read_brief); must read at least three sources; Test budget EUR 20,000 and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions, not company figures; Partly public financial data: note what cannot be found or reconciled; Must first establish how far RATIONAL already reaches individual buyers, not assume it. Alternatives: No expansion: remain focused on professional commercial kitchens (status quo); Consumer product: develop a home-cook version of combi-steamer technology sold direct to households; Route-to-market change: keep the same product but sell to home cooks via existing retail or online channels; Adjacent customer group: small professional or prosumer segments (caterers, bakeries, premium restaurants, serious home enthusiasts) rather than mass home cooks; Partnership or licensing: license the core steam/combi technology to an appliance maker for a home product, keeping the professional business; Hybrid: a small consumer line used to build brand and data while the core stays commercial.
Searched for "RATIONAL consumer home cooking iCombi home appliance"; found rational-ir-potential, rational-wiki-icombi90, rational-anova-electrolux.

T1: Home cooks who want restaurant-quality results but lack skill would pay a premium for a combi-steamer sold as an easy-to-use appliance, so RATIONAL could earn premium margins by controlling the design and brand of a home version of its existing steam-and-convection technology. Who benefits: Affluent home cooks and serious amateurs who want consistent results; RATIONAL, if it captures the premium margin and brand halo.. Why behaviour changes: Steam-convection cooking removes much of the skill and timing guesswork that home cooks face, so the professional technology becomes a visible reason to buy rather than a technical spec.. How value is captured: RATIONAL sells a branded home unit direct or through premium retail at a price above mass kitchen appliances, keeping design, software and service in-house.. Assumptions: Home cooks will pay a large premium over mass appliances for professional-grade results; Kitchen space and installation do not block purchase at the target price; RATIONAL can build consumer distribution and support without damaging its professional brand; The commercial technology can be shrunk and made cheaply enough for a home price point. Predictions: Stated willingness to pay for a home unit at the target price is high among affluent cooks who already own premium appliances; Pre-orders or deposits at a test price exceed a set threshold in a landing-page test; Buyers cite ease of consistent results rather than professional credentials as the main reason to buy.

T2: Home cooking is used too infrequently and in too constrained a space for a commercial-grade combi-steamer to earn back its cost, so a consumer product would sell in small volumes and mainly serve as a brand showcase; the professional business keeps the real value. Who benefits: Professional kitchens, which keep RATIONAL's focus, service network and margins; home buyers gain little beyond novelty.. Why behaviour changes: Home cooks cook a few times a week, value counter space and simplicity, and compare a combi-steamer against cheaper multi-cookers, so the purchase rarely reaches the price where a premium unit pays back.. How value is captured: RATIONAL stays with commercial sales, where a unit is used all day and the return on investment is measurable; any home activity earns little beyond brand awareness.. Assumptions: Home use frequency is far below commercial use, so per-use value is low; Home buyers are price-sensitive relative to the cost of a professional-grade unit; Space and installation constraints limit the addressable home market; Competing home appliances already cover most of the steam-cooking use case. Predictions: Stated purchase intent falls sharply once the price is shown alongside alternatives; Home buyers who own a multi-cooker rarely cite a need the combi-steamer would meet; Consumer-line sales stay a small share of total revenue even after launch.

T1 supports, from rational-anova-electrolux (analogy): "On February 6, 2017, Anova was acquired by Electrolux , a home appliance company, for a total of US$250 million.". Does not show: This is a different company selling a cheaper sous-vide device, not RATIONAL. It shows that a home appliance maker paid for a precision-cooking brand, which makes a premium home niche look commercially valuable. It does not show that home cooks would buy a combi-steamer, what they would pay, or whether RATIONAL could sell one..

T2 neutral, from rational-wiki-icombi90 (market_fact): "Combi ovens (iCombi product line) generate approximately 90% of Rational's appliance sales, while about 10% comes from the iVario series and newly added iHexagon appliances.". Does not show: The source gives a product-mix share, not customer type, so it does not show that sales are professional or that home use is weak. It is a secondary summary with an unknown date. It cannot test whether a home unit would pay back. It only shows that the company's appliance revenue is concentrated in one product family..
Looked for evidence against T2: "home consumers buy combi steam oven premium appliance willingness to pay"; found rational-anova-oven, rational-combi-countertop, rational-wiki-icombi90.

T2 contradicts, from rational-combi-countertop (market_fact): "These countertop appliances have the same characteristic changes as the full-size household appliances, except that they are smaller, and cost significantly less than a full-size oven.". Does not show: The source does not give sales volumes, brands, prices, geography or whether home buyers use these units often. It says nothing about RATIONAL, and a cheaper countertop unit may not show that a premium professional-grade home unit would pay back. It weakens my claim that home use is too rare or space-limited to justify a product, but does not settle it..

Test "Premium home unit landing-page and deposit test" between T1; T2. Method: Run a paid-traffic landing page for a home combi-steamer concept shown at three proposed price points, with a refundable deposit option. Use a fictitious brand or unlabelled concept so intent is not biased by the RATIONAL name. Also include a short survey on current appliances and cooking frequency.. Sample: Proposed: about 3,000 qualified visitors from German-speaking and Dutch home-cooking audiences who own premium kitchen appliances (estimated, to be checked against actual traffic costs).. Measure: Share of visitors who place a refundable deposit at each price point; stated purchase intent; reported cooking frequency per week; reason for not buying.. Predictions: T1: A meaningful share of qualified visitors deposit at the premium price, with deposits stable across the top price point and the main stated reason being consistent results rather than credentials.; T2: Deposits fall sharply as price rises, most visitors cook only a few times a week, and the main stated reasons are counter space, cost against multi-cookers and no clear need.. Decision rule: Proposed threshold: if at least 2% of qualified visitors deposit at the premium price and at least half of depositors say they cook 4 or more times a week, keep T1 and scope a consumer prototype. If below 0.5% at premium price, or most cook under twice a week, reject T1 and stay with professional kitchens. Between these, keep both open and run a second test.. Cost: 14000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T2: Stay with professional kitchens as the main business. Do not build a full home-cook product now. If the board wants to learn about home demand, run the proposed deposit test (EUR 14,000 of the EUR 20,000 budget, six weeks) and make any consumer move conditional on its result. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: likely.

T1 kept: No real evidence was added this round. The only new item is a SIMULATED what-if on installation coordination, which I have not used as evidence. T1 stays open and untested. The countertop combi-steamer source weakens T2's space argument but says nothing about RATIONAL or premium pricing. New claim: none. Evidence: rational-combi-countertop.

T2 kept: I considered SYN-RATIONAL-UPDATE as a what-if only. It is a SIMULATED result and I do not cite it as evidence. Even if it were real, it concerns installation friction in one recruited group, not the home use frequency or cost-to-value that T2 depends on, so it would not change T2. T2 stays the favoured theory on the thin real evidence, and the deposit test is still the decisive next step. New claim: none. Evidence: rational-ir-potential.

T1 kept: What-if only, per the stage instruction: if SYN-RATIONAL-UPDATE were real, it would show that installation coordination changes reservations in one recruited group (72 vs 32 per 400). For T1 that means only that premium-buyer friction matters, and the test is about a bundled service, not about the appliance's demand or price. It would not confirm that home cooks pay a premium for the product. Nothing here is real data; I do not change my belief and I do not cite it in the finish. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-RATIONAL-UPDATE.

Recommendation: Stay focused on professional kitchens. Do not build a full home-cook product now. Before any consumer move, run the proposed refundable-deposit test (about EUR 14,000 of the EUR 20,000 budget, six weeks) and let its pre-agreed threshold decide. Target customer: Professional kitchens remain the target. Home cooks are an unproven, separate test, not a current segment.. Value proposition: For professional kitchens: the combi-steamer's measurable performance in daily commercial use. No home value proposition is supported by the evidence I read.. Favoured theory: T2. Next action: Scope the proposed landing-page and deposit test with an unlabelled concept at three price points, and agree thresholds before running it: keep the consumer option open only if at least 2% of qualified visitors deposit at the premium price and at least half of depositors cook four or more times a week (both proposed, not observed).. Uncertainty: Home-demand evidence is very thin. No source I read measures home buyers, willingness to pay or home use frequency. The 4.8 million figure is a company estimate. The 90% iCombi share is a secondary summary of unknown date. Anova's sale is an analogy. I could not find or reconcile RATIONAL's financial data by channel or customer type. No SIMULATED result is used as evidence.. Would change if: The deposit test clears the proposed thresholds at the premium price, with depositors reporting frequent use; Public data shows premium countertop combi-steamers selling in volume near a professional unit's cost; RATIONAL's own disclosures show a home or prosumer channel reaching individual buyers at scale; Reliable data shows professional demand saturating, leaving growth only in adjacent segments; A licensing partner offers a home product that needs no RATIONAL capital or brand risk. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: likely.

case.question: Should Electrolux Professional Group develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing professional laundry offering? What evidence would justify that investment?
case.source_limits: Evidence is limited to the case dossier: each source shows everything the dossier holds for it, often a short excerpt, not the whole original. Results marked simulated are what-if evidence, not real observations.

sources.excerpt: In addition, residential customers are increasingly demanding commercial-quality products for the home, and our machines represent a compelling fit for this select but growing segment of the residential market.
Over 40,000 cycles for long‑term investment that outlasts any alternative in the market Built by Professionals for the Professionals : for reliable quality and robustness
Consumer‑operated setups enable residents, guests or members to run their own laundry in multi‑family buildings, student housing, campsites, marinas, gyms or staff facilities.

Electrolux Professional provides integrated solutions designed for different formats – laundromats, bungalows and consumer‑operated – combining reliability, resource efficiency and serviceability to maximize uptime and ROI.

events.text: Objective: Decide whether Electrolux Professional Group should invest in a differentiated proposition for a specific use case that reaches buyers beyond its professional laundry offering, and identify what evidence would justify that investment rather than assuming demand.. Constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only; no company contact or intentions assumed; Some financial and contractual detail may be non-public and must be reported as not found; Test budget of 20000 EUR and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions, not company figures; Searches are limited to 8 in total, with 1 kept for challenge; Company assertions are not proof of demand. Alternatives: No expansion: stay purely professional B2B in commercial laundry and food service; Product redesign: adapt existing professional machines, for example compact or lower-noise models, for small-business or prosumer buyers without changing channel; Different route to buyers: sell existing products through retail, direct-to-consumer or partner channels; Different customer group: target a specific adjacent segment such as small hospitality, care homes, student housing or independent laundrette operators, rather than households; Brand licensing: license the professional brand to a consumer appliance maker and earn royalties without running consumer channels; Service or subscription model: lease or service existing professional equipment for micro-businesses.
Searched for "Electrolux Professional consumer direct sales individual buyers"; found epro-consumer-operated, epro-selfservice-formats, epro-compact-power-cycles.

T1: EPG's existing reach to individual buyers runs through property owners and small operators who buy self-service laundry for residents or guests, not through households buying for their own home. The compact professional machine is useful as a route into that segment, not as a consumer product. Who benefits: Electrolux Professional, through sales of commercial machines to property owners, campsite and marina operators, and student housing managers who need turnkey self-service laundry.. Why behaviour changes: Property owners and operators want to offer laundry as an amenity or income source without staffing it. Reliability and serviceability (the company's stated ROI framing) reduce their risk of downtime and complaints, so they buy commercial-grade equipment over cheaper residential machines.. How value is captured: Equipment sale plus service and spare parts over the machine's life. The company's own claim of over 40,000 cycles implies a long replacement cycle that supports a premium price and recurring service revenue.. Assumptions: Buyers are business or property operators, not individual households; Uptime and serviceability drive purchase decisions more than purchase price; Consumer-operated setups are a meaningful share of EPG's sales, not a marginal line; Residents pay per use or the operator recovers cost, so demand depends on property-level economics. Predictions: Sales growth in self-service formats tracks property-operator investment cycles, not household purchasing; Buyers ask first about service response times and uptime guarantees in tenders; A household-branded version of the same machine would sell poorly to households without an operator; Revenue share of consumer-operated formats is disclosed in segment reporting or investor material, which would confirm or limit scale.

T2: Households will buy a compact, long-life professional-grade washer-dryer for their own home if it is positioned on durability and total cost of ownership rather than as a commercial machine, so a prosumer version could reach individual buyers directly. Who benefits: Affluent households and home-workers who replace consumer machines often and want longevity, and EPG if a premium prosumer line sells through retail or direct channels.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers who judge appliances by lifetime cost and repair frequency may prefer a machine rated for tens of thousands of cycles over a cheaper residential model, once they know the professional build exists. This is a cause that differs from the operator-led one: the buying unit is the household, and the driver is perceived durability, not uptime for a business.. How value is captured: A price premium on a prosumer SKU sold through retail or direct channels, with the same engineering platform as the professional range to reduce development cost.. Assumptions: Households value cycle life and robustness enough to pay a premium over residential machines; Home installation constraints (space, water, power, noise, drainage) do not block purchase; Professional-grade machines are not too loud or large for home use; Brand recognition in consumer channels transfers from commercial credibility. Predictions: Consumer reviews and search interest for professional-grade home machines are mostly about durability, not features; A pilot listing in a consumer retailer would sell at a premium only in households that already buy premium appliances; Demand falls sharply when installation or noise requirements are included in the price comparison; Sales would be concentrated in a small share of households, not mass market.

T1 supports, from epro-consumer-operated (company_assertion): "Consumer‑operated setups enable residents, guests or members to run their own laundry in multi‑family buildings, student housing, campsites, marinas, gyms or staff facilities.". Does not show: It does not show who buys the machines, what share of EPG revenue comes from these formats, or whether property operators decide on uptime rather than price. It is a marketing description of use settings, not sales data..

T2 neutral, from epro-compact-power-cycles (company_assertion): "Over 40,000 cycles for long‑term investment that outlasts any alternative in the market Built by Professionals for the Professionals : for reliable quality and robustness". Does not show: The page is aimed at professionals ('Built by Professionals for the Professionals'), so it says nothing about households wanting this machine. The 40,000-cycle figure is an unverified company claim with no test method. It does not show consumer demand, price tolerance, or installation feasibility in a home..

Looked for evidence against T1: "self-service laundry operator sales share revenue consumer-operated residential demand decline"; found epro-consumer-operated, epro-selfservice-formats, epro-alliance-residential-segment.

T2 supports, from epro-alliance-residential-segment (company_assertion): "residential customers are increasingly demanding commercial-quality products for the home, and our machines represent a compelling fit for this select but growing segment of the residential market.". Does not show: This is a competitor's own prospectus claim about North America, not measured demand. The words 'select' and 'growing' are not sized. It does not show the price premium, the share of sales, or whether EPG's European products would fit. It is a claim about a segment, not proof that the segment buys..

Test "Household pre-order and operator quote test for a compact professional washer-dryer" between T1; T2. Method: Run two parallel low-cost demand probes in one EU market. (a) Household probe: show a prosumer-positioned compact machine (durability and cycle-life message, no commercial branding) to homeowners on a landing page with a refundable deposit and a space, water, drainage and noise checklist. (b) Operator probe: send the same spec to property managers, campsite and student-housing operators with a request for a quote and a service-level question. Compare deposit conversion and quote requests.. Sample: Proposed: about 300 household visitors recruited through paid search and home-appliance forums, plus 25 to 40 property and campsite operators reached through direct outreach and trade contacts.. Measure: Household: share of visitors who pay a refundable deposit after seeing the installation checklist. Operator: number of formal quote requests and whether uptime or service response time is raised as the first question.. Predictions: T1: Operator quote requests are numerous and lead with uptime and service questions; household deposits are few and fall away once installation requirements are shown.; T2: Household deposits are meaningful, especially among premium appliance buyers, and the durability message drives clicks more than the installation checklist deters them.. Decision rule: Proposed threshold: if household deposit conversion is at least 3 percent of qualified visitors after the checklist, and at least 8 operator quote requests are received, treat T2 as worth a further prosumer feasibility study. If household deposits are under 1 percent and operator quotes are at least 8, keep T1 as the working theory and drop the household line. If both are below threshold, decline further investment in either proposition.. Cost: 14000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not launch a household-branded consumer product now. Keep the self-service and property-operator route as the working theory, since EPG's own pages describe it, and test the household prosumer idea cheaply before any investment. Revisit only if the household probe clears its threshold. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Do not invest now in a household-branded consumer proposition. Treat EPG's existing reach as property-operator and self-service formats (multi-family buildings, student housing, campsites, marinas, gyms, staff facilities), and test the household prosumer idea cheaply before committing any development budget. The evidence is almost entirely company marketing, so it cannot show how large these formats are or whether households would buy. Target customer: Property owners, student-housing and campsite operators, and marina or gym managers who offer laundry to residents or guests and need reliable, serviceable machines.. Value proposition: Turnkey self-service laundry with commercial reliability, low downtime and easy service, where the operator's risk of complaints and breakdowns is the main concern. The 40,000-cycle claim is supporting detail, not proof.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed two-probe test (X1): a household prosumer landing page with a refundable deposit and installation checklist, plus an operator quote-request probe. Budget 14,000 EUR, 10 weeks, both proposed and estimated. Before running it, request EPG's segment revenue split for consumer-operated formats, which is not in the public sources I read.. Uncertainty: Several things are unknown. I could not find EPG's revenue or sales share for self-service and consumer-operated formats, nor its margins or contract terms. The Compact Power launch is recent and its 40,000-cycle claim has no published test method. The Alliance residential claim is a North American competitor's prospectus statement, not measured demand, and does not transfer directly to EU households. Household demand for a professional-grade machine is untested. My belief in T1 is likely only because the company's own pages describe that use; it has not been checked against sales data.. Would change if: Household deposit conversion in the probe is at least 3 percent of qualified visitors after the installation checklist, which would move T2 up and justify a prosumer feasibility study; Segment reporting or an analyst source shows consumer-operated formats are a marginal share of sales, which would weaken T1 and make the operator route less worth building around; Operator quotes lead with price rather than uptime or service, which would contradict the T1 prediction about buyer priorities; A verified source shows EU households are unwilling to fit professional machines for space, noise or drainage reasons, which would close the household line; EPG's segment data shows the self-service line is large and growing with a clear buyer profile, which would strengthen the case for a product focused on property operators. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Consumer‑operated setups enable residents, guests or members to run their own laundry in multi‑family buildings, student housing, campsites, marinas, gyms or staff facilities.
