events.text: Objective: Decide whether Electrolux Professional Group should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for one specific use case beyond its professional laundry offering, and identify what evidence would justify that investment rather than staying B2B-only.. Constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only; no company contact or intentions assumed; Financial and contractual detail may be non-public; state the gaps; Test budget 20000 EUR and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions; Search budget of 8 searches, 7 remaining, plus 1 kept-for-challenge slot; Company assertions are not proof of consumer demand; Must verify what EPG already sells to individual buyers rather than assume. Alternatives: No expansion: stay purely professional, focused on commercial laundry and food-service core; Route change: sell existing professional-grade machines to individual buyers through retail or online channels with minimal product change; Product redesign: a compact machine adapted for one home use case such as small apartments; Different customer group: small businesses or micro-enterprises such as home-based service providers or small laundromats rather than consumers; Licensing: license professional technology or brand to a consumer appliance maker and earn royalties without direct retail; Lease or service model: rent professional-grade units to households or small operators with maintenance included.
Searched for "Electrolux Professional consumer sales individual buyers household"; found epro-consumer-operated, epro-selfservice-formats, epro-ec-study-uk-wtp.

T1: EPG's realistic route to individual buyers is through shared, consumer-operated laundry in multi-family buildings, campsites and similar sites, where the building or site operator buys the machines and residents pay per wash. The consumer buys a service, not the machine. Who benefits: Building owners, property managers and campsite or marina operators who want a revenue-generating or amenity laundry without staffing it; EPG earns equipment and service revenue from them.. Why behaviour changes: Residents without space, or without a home machine, will pay per cycle for convenient laundry on site. The operator gains income and avoids labour costs, so the operator, not the household, makes the purchase decision.. How value is captured: EPG sells professional machines and recurring service contracts to operators, and may take a share of per-cycle payment systems. Value sits with the operator relationship, which is already EPG's B2B channel.. Assumptions: Operators prefer professional-grade machines because of uptime and serviceability, and will pay a premium for them; Residents in multi-family buildings lack home laundry or accept paying per cycle; Operators buy through existing EPG sales channels, so no consumer retail is needed. Predictions: Sales growth in EPG self-service lines will come from operator and property-manager accounts, not from households buying directly; Operators will accept per-cycle payment pricing that covers machine and service cost within a fixed payback period; A pilot with one operator will show usage per machine per week above a set break-even level.

T2: Households will pay a premium for a domestic appliance that is advertised as lasting longer and carrying a longer warranty, so a professional-grade durability position sold directly to households could earn premium prices. Who benefits: Households that want fewer replacements and lower lifetime cost; a maker that can credibly claim longevity earns a price premium.. Why behaviour changes: Buyers judge appliances by expected lifetime and repair risk. When durability is stated and backed by a longer guarantee, they are willing to pay more upfront to avoid replacement costs.. How value is captured: EPG would sell a compact or domestic-adapted machine at a premium over mass-market rivals, supported by a longer warranty and service network built from its professional channel.. Assumptions: Stated willingness to pay for durability in surveys carries over to actual purchases; Professional reliability can be delivered in a domestic-sized product at a cost that allows a premium; Consumers can verify durability claims before buying or trust the warranty. Predictions: Households shown a longer-warranty, durability-labelled model will choose it at a higher price than an otherwise identical standard model in a controlled price test; Stated premium will be smaller in actual purchase behaviour than in survey answers; Premium uptake will be concentrated in households that already report replacing appliances early.

T1 supports, from epro-consumer-operated (company_assertion): "Consumer‑operated setups enable residents, guests or members to run their own laundry in multi‑family buildings, student housing, campsites, marinas, gyms or staff facilities.". Does not show: Does not show that operators buy these machines, how many units are sold, what prices residents pay per cycle, or whether any households buy machines themselves. It is a product page written by the company..

T2 supports, from epro-ec-study-uk-wtp (independent_study): "more than eight out of ten consumers would be willing to pay extra for household electrical appliances that are advertised to last longer and have a longer commercial guarantee or warranty. On average they would be willing to pay 10% more.". Does not show: Stated willingness to pay in a survey and focus group in England and Wales in 2018; not observed purchases, not laundry appliances specifically, not EPG products, and not whether a premium would hold against cheaper rivals. Stated premiums usually overstate actual behaviour..
Looked for evidence against T1: "shared laundry operators residents pay per cycle usage decline"; found epro-eu-installed-base, epro-consumer-operated, epro-compact-power-cycles.

T1 contradicts, from epro-eu-installed-base (market_fact): "In 2020, 175 million washing machines and washer-dryers were in use in the EU27.". Does not show: Does not say how many of these are in households versus shared or communal facilities, nor how many households lack a machine. It weakly undercuts the assumption that residents lack home laundry, but does not test whether shared-laundry operators buy or whether residents pay per cycle..

Test "Operator pilot versus durability price test" between T1; T2. Method: Two parallel low-cost probes. (a) T1: place or simulate one consumer-operated pay-per-cycle laundry with a partner property operator for 8 weeks and record cycles per machine per week and whether the operator would sign a purchase. (b) T2: online or in-store choice test of a durability-labelled domestic-sized model versus an otherwise identical standard model at a 10% higher price, with randomised price and warranty framing, measuring actual choice rather than stated intent.. Sample: T1: one to three partner multi-family or campsite sites, residents using the machine (proposed). T2: about 600 households in one or two EU markets via a panel or a retailer test (proposed estimate).. Measure: T1: cycles per machine per week, operator's written purchase intent, per-cycle price residents accept. T2: share choosing the durability-labelled model at the premium price, versus control.. Predictions: T1: Usage at or above the operator's break-even cycle rate within 8 weeks, and at least one operator states a purchase intent for a fleet or renewal.; T2: Choice share for the durability model at the 10% premium is well below stated survey intent (for example under 20%), indicating stated premiums overstate behaviour and the premium is fragile.. Decision rule: Pursue T1 only if at least two sites reach the proposed break-even cycle rate and one operator gives a written purchase intent. Pursue T2 only if the durability model wins at least 25% share at the 10% premium versus control. Otherwise stay B2B-only (no consumer proposition).. Cost: 18000 euros, 12 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not launch a consumer product now. The only consumer-facing channel EPG evidently uses is consumer-operated laundry sold to building and site operators, which is B2B with resident payment. Test that channel first with a small operator pilot. Treat a direct household durability premium as unproven. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: unlikely.

T2 rejected: Reasoning as if the SIMULATED result were real (it is not, and is not evidence): in a durability-and-repairability description arm, 32 of 400 buyers reserved (8%), against 72 of 400 (18%) in a performance-and-price arm, with identical product, price and warranty. Durability wording did not raise uptake in this framing, so the claim that households pay a premium for durability is not supported in this form. The survey finding (EC study, 10% stated WTP) remains stated intent only. The result tests description, not lifetime, delivery or market size, and says nothing about T1. New claim: Households do not reliably pay a durability premium for a domestic appliance from a professional-derived brand when the durability message is the lead; any premium is unproven and likely overstated by stated-preference surveys.. Evidence: epro-ec-study-uk-wtp; SYN-EPRO-UPDATE.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a consumer product now. The public evidence shows EPG reaching individual users only indirectly, through consumer-operated laundry that building, campsite and similar operators buy and residents pay to use. Test that operator channel before anything else. Treat a direct household durability premium as unproven. Target customer: Property and site operators (multi-family housing, student housing, campsites, marinas) who buy self-service laundry; residents are the end users but not the buyer.. Value proposition: Professional-grade machines with uptime, serviceability and resource efficiency, sold to operators who earn per-cycle revenue or provide an amenity without staffing it. For households, no proposition is recommended yet.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run a small operator pilot (proposed: one to three partner sites, about 8 weeks, within a EUR 18,000 and 12-week envelope, all figures estimated). Measure cycles per machine per week against an operator break-even rate and whether an operator gives written purchase intent. Pursue the operator channel only if at least two sites reach break-even and one operator commits in writing. Separately, a household durability test is worth running only if the premium is re-tested as actual choice, not survey intent.. Uncertainty: Little of this is verified. EPG's consumer-operated offer is documented only by its own product pages, which give no sales volumes, unit counts, prices, margins or contract terms; these are not public and were not found. The 175 million EU washing machines figure is a 2020 aggregate and does not show how many are in households versus shared facilities. The 10% stated premium is from a 2018 UK-focused survey of stated intent, not purchases. I found no independent evidence on operator payback or resident per-cycle willingness to pay. I did not use the simulated update as evidence.. Would change if: Public or disclosed data showing EPG unit sales or revenue in consumer-operated laundry, which would show whether the operator channel already scales; A partner operator refusing to commit to any purchase or payback threshold in the pilot, which would weaken T1; Operator pilot cycle rates below break-even across sites, which would reject T1 in its current form; Evidence that households without home laundry are a large, reachable group willing to pay per cycle, which would open a consumer route; A real, non-stated test showing a durability premium holds at scale, which would revive a product-redesign option. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: unlikely.

case.question: Should Electrolux Professional Group develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing professional laundry offering? What evidence would justify that investment?
case.source_limits: Evidence is limited to the case dossier: each source shows everything the dossier holds for it, often a short excerpt, not the whole original. Results marked simulated are what-if evidence, not real observations.

events.text: The investigation stopped before a recommendation (repeated errors).

case.question: Should RATIONAL develop a differentiated proposition for home cooks, building on its commercial combi-steamer technology, or stay with professional kitchens? What evidence would justify either choice?
case.source_limits: Evidence is limited to the case dossier: each source shows everything the dossier holds for it, often a short excerpt, not the whole original. Results marked simulated are what-if evidence, not real observations.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 72 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 32 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.
On February 6, 2017, Anova was acquired by Electrolux , a home appliance company, for a total of US$250 million.

Subsequent products included the Anova Precision Cooker Nano and the Anova Precision Oven, a countertop combi oven that supported both steam and convection cooking methods and could be used either alongside other Precision Cooker products or by itself.
Germany: RATIONAL AG , Gaggenau Hausgeräte , PALUX, Convotherm, MKN, ELOMA, Miele , AEG (part of Electrolux), Bosch.
From 1978 onwards, the company concentrated solely on combi steamers and discontinued all other product lines.
Combi ovens (iCombi product line) generate approximately 90% of Rational's appliance sales, while about 10% comes from the iVario series and newly added iHexagon appliances.

events.text: Objective: Decide whether RATIONAL AG should build a differentiated proposition for home cooks on its combi-steamer technology, or keep its focus on professional kitchens, and identify what evidence would justify each choice. Establish first how far RATIONAL already reaches individual buyers.. Constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only; no company contact or insight into intentions; Company financials are partly public; gaps and non-reconcilable figures must be stated, not filled in; Test budget of EUR 20,000 and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions, not company figures; Search budget of 8 searches (7 remaining); must read at least three sources; No SIMULATED results may be cited in the final recommendation; Company claims about demand are not proof of demand. Alternatives: A. No expansion: remain purely professional-kitchen focused, with optional monitoring of consumer interest; B. Consumer redesign: a smaller, simpler or differently priced combi-steamer sold directly to home cooks; C. Different route to buyers: same product sold via appliance retailers, online marketplaces or premium kitchen brands; D. Different customer group: prosumers, serious home bakers or small food businesses rather than general home cooks; E. Adjacent proposition: software, recipes or service subscriptions on the existing connected-oven platform, hardware unchanged; F. Licensing or partnering: license cooking-control technology or programs to a consumer appliance maker for royalties.
Searched for "RATIONAL combi-steamer home cooks consumer products"; found rational-wiki-1978, rational-wiki-icombi90, rational-combi-makers.

T1: Home cooks who are serious about cooking would pay a premium for a compact professional-grade steamer because it is perceived as a mark of cooking skill, so a maker with a proven professional brand could earn premium prices in the home segment. Who benefits: Serious home cooks who want restaurant-quality results and identify with professional equipment; RATIONAL, which would gain a higher-margin consumer line from its existing brand and technology.. Why behaviour changes: Owning professional equipment signals competence and taste, so buyers accept a high price for a device they would use only at home. Brand reputation from commercial kitchens transfers to the consumer product and reduces perceived risk.. How value is captured: RATIONAL sets a premium price on a branded home unit sold through its own channel or premium kitchen retailers, keeping the margin that a generic appliance maker would lose to retail discounting.. Assumptions: A meaningful group of home cooks exists who are willing to pay a large premium over mainstream built-in ovens; The brand carries consumer status value, not only professional credibility; A smaller unit can deliver the core steaming and combi results at home. Predictions: Pre-orders or waitlist sign-ups at a premium price point (estimated above 2x a mainstream built-in oven) will be concentrated among existing commercial-brand awareness groups such as chefs and enthusiasts; Conversion falls sharply when the same unit is shown at mainstream appliance prices; Stated willingness to pay is higher for the RATIONAL brand than for an unbranded equivalent.

T2: Home cooks do not buy combi-steamers mainly because of cooking results. The binding constraint is installation and channel: built-in appliance slots, kitchen fit and installer networks are controlled by incumbent home-appliance makers, so a commercial-kitchen maker captures little value by going direct and does better by licensing its technology into an existing home-appliance channel. Who benefits: Incumbent home-appliance makers (for example Miele, Bosch, BSH/Gaggenau) that already hold the built-in slot and retail shelf; RATIONAL would benefit only through licence income rather than selling to consumers directly.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers buy what fits their built-in kitchen and what their installer or retailer recommends. A new brand selling a separate steam appliance faces a fit and service barrier, so purchase depends on the channel offering installation, warranty and servicing.. How value is captured: RATIONAL earns per-unit royalties or a supply fee from a home-appliance partner that already owns installation, service and retail, instead of carrying the cost of consumer marketing, service networks and returns.. Assumptions: Home-appliance makers already sell built-in steam or combi ovens to consumers and would license commercial cooking-control technology; Installation and after-sales service are the main purchase barriers for built-in kitchen appliances; Licensing terms would leave RATIONAL with a meaningful share of the value. Predictions: Consumer sales of combi and steam built-in units track the number of installer and retail partners in a market more closely than advertising spend; Home-appliance makers that already sell steam ovens (such as Miele, Bosch, Gaggenau, AEG) hold most of the installed base; A direct-to-consumer launch without installer coverage shows low conversion even at a modest price.

T1 neutral, from rational-combi-makers (market_fact): "Germany: RATIONAL AG , Gaggenau Hausgeräte , PALUX, Convotherm, MKN, ELOMA, Miele , AEG (part of Electrolux), Bosch.". Does not show: Whether any of these makers sell combi-steamers to households, at what price, or whether a premium brand earns extra willingness to pay from home cooks. The list names makers in the category; it says nothing about demand or price..

T2 supports, from rational-combi-makers (market_fact): "Germany: RATIONAL AG , Gaggenau Hausgeräte , PALUX, Convotherm, MKN, ELOMA, Miele , AEG (part of Electrolux), Bosch.". Does not show: Installed base, installer or retail coverage, or how much of the household channel each maker controls. It shows that home-appliance makers (Gaggenau Hausgeräte, Miele, AEG, Bosch) are listed alongside RATIONAL in the combi-steamer category, which is consistent with incumbents being present, but not that installation is the binding barrier..

Looked for evidence against T2: "home appliance makers combi steam oven consumer sales installation service direct-to-consumer online sales"; found rational-wiki-icombi90, rational-anova-oven, rational-ir-customers.

T2 contradicts, from rational-anova-oven (market_fact): "Subsequent products included the Anova Precision Cooker Nano and the Anova Precision Oven, a countertop combi oven that supported both steam and convection cooking methods and could be used either alongside other Precision Cooker products or by itself.". Does not show: Sales volume, customer retention, or whether the oven was commercially successful. It shows a countertop combi oven was sold to home users without built-in installation, which weakens T2's claim that installation is the binding barrier, but not the claim that channel control matters for built-in units..

Test "Format, price and channel landing-page test with paid-intent sign-up" between T1; T2. Method: Run a fake-door test: three landing pages describing a home steam-cooking unit, each with a pre-order or waitlist button requiring a refundable deposit. Variants: (a) countertop plug-in unit at a premium price; (b) built-in unit requiring a certified installer at the same premium price; (c) countertop unit at a mainstream price. Traffic is bought through paid search and social targeting to home cooks who already buy premium kitchen tools. Brand is shown in half of each variant's traffic, unbranded in the other half, to separate brand effect from format and price effect. Deposits are refunded to all sign-ups at test end.. Sample: Proposed: about 6,000 qualified visitors across variants and brand conditions (about 1,000 per cell), drawn from an estimated EUR 12,000 of paid traffic. Estimated, not observed.. Measure: Deposit sign-up rate per qualified visitor, by variant and brand condition, with a 95% confidence interval. Secondary: share of sign-ups who give a postcode inside the installer coverage area for variant (b).. Predictions: T1: Sign-up rate at the premium price is high enough to justify a product, the branded condition beats the unbranded condition clearly, and the mainstream-price variant (c) converts far below the premium variant (a). Format (a) versus (b) makes little difference.; T2: Sign-up rate for the built-in variant (b) falls well below the countertop variant (a) at the same price, mainly for visitors outside installer coverage. Brand effect is small. Channel and installation, not price or brand, drive the gap.. Decision rule: Proposed threshold. Favour T1 if the premium countertop sign-up rate is at least 3% and the branded condition is at least 1.5 times the unbranded rate, while the mainstream-price rate is under half the premium rate. Favour T2 if the built-in variant's sign-up rate is under one-third of the countertop variant's and the gap is concentrated outside installer coverage, with brand difference under 1.2 times. If neither threshold is met, treat both theories as unsupported and do not commit to a consumer product. Note: a fake-door test measures stated intent, which overstates purchase; the 3% threshold is a proposed screen, not a demand estimate.. Cost: 14000 euros, 6 weeks.

Looked for evidence against T1: "home cooks premium brand willingness to pay countertop steam oven price sensitivity consumer appliance"; found rational-anova-oven, rational-combi-countertop, rational-anova-electrolux.

T2 supports, from rational-anova-electrolux (market_fact): "On February 6, 2017, Anova was acquired by Electrolux , a home appliance company, for a total of US$250 million.". Does not show: Why Electrolux paid, what share of the price reflected brand, technology or channel, or whether the acquisition paid off. It shows a home-appliance incumbent valued a consumer cooking brand enough to buy it, which fits value sitting with incumbents who control consumer access, but it does not establish that installation or channel is the binding barrier..

Favours T2: Keep the professional-kitchen focus as the base case. Do not build a consumer-branded home product on current evidence. If a consumer route is pursued, the evidence so far favours licensing or partnering with an incumbent that already controls installation and retail (option F) over a direct RATIONAL consumer line. Run the proposed format and channel test (X1) before committing to either route. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T2 kept: I reviewed a SIMULATED offer test as a what-if. If it were real, it would show installation coordination roughly doubling reservations (about 18% versus 8%), which would support T2's claim that installation friction changes choice. Because it is simulated and cites no real data, it does not change my belief and is excluded from the evidence base. The real evidence (the Anova countertop oven and the Electrolux acquisition) bears on T2 only indirectly. T2 stays uncertain; the channel-versus-brand question is still open. New claim: none. Evidence: rational-anova-electrolux; rational-anova-oven.

T1 kept: Reviewed the SIMULATED coordination offer test as a what-if. It bears mainly on installation friction, not on brand or price, so it does not test T1. T1 remains uncertain: I have no real evidence of a home-cook price premium or brand effect. The proposed test X1 is what would test it. New claim: none. Evidence: rational-combi-makers; rational-anova-oven.

T2 kept: No further revision. T2 remains uncertain. The only new item this round is a SIMULATED what-if, which I have not treated as evidence. The real evidence bears on T2 only indirectly (Anova countertop oven, Electrolux acquisition). Next step is the proposed test X1 and the annual-report check, not a belief change. New claim: none. Evidence: rational-anova-electrolux.
The investigation stopped before a recommendation (repeated errors).

case.question: Should RATIONAL develop a differentiated proposition for home cooks, building on its commercial combi-steamer technology, or stay with professional kitchens? What evidence would justify either choice?
case.source_limits: Evidence is limited to the case dossier: each source shows everything the dossier holds for it, often a short excerpt, not the whole original. Results marked simulated are what-if evidence, not real observations.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. In this simulated warehouse test, a new label printer reduced packing errors slightly. Nothing about wearers or buyers was measured.

Subsequent products included the Anova Precision Cooker Nano and the Anova Precision Oven, a countertop combi oven that supported both steam and convection cooking methods and could be used either alongside other Precision Cooker products or by itself.
These countertop appliances have the same characteristic changes as the full-size household appliances, except that they are smaller, and cost significantly less than a full-size oven.

The customer base ranges from restaurants and hotels, company canteens, hospitals, schools, universities, the military, prisons and retirement homes to fast-food restaurants, party services, supermarkets, bakeries and snack bars, butchers, petrol stations and delivery services, including so-called ghost kitchens.
RATIONAL AG is the global market and technology leader for innovative cooking systems in commercial food preparation.

events.text: Objective: Decide whether RATIONAL AG should build a differentiated proposition for home cooks using its combi-steamer technology, or keep its focus on professional kitchens. Identify what public evidence would justify either choice, and what the company already does with individual buyers, which the brief does not tell us.. Constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only; no company contact or insider intentions; Search budget: 8 searches total (7 remaining after read_brief); Test budget 20,000 EUR and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions, not company figures; Partly public financial data: report what cannot be found or reconciled; No simulated results may be cited as evidence in finish; Company-issued claims are not proof of consumer demand. Alternatives: A. No expansion: stay with professional kitchens and deepen commercial channel, service and software; B. Consumer-facing product extension: a smaller, cheaper or redesigned combi-steamer for home kitchens sold under the existing brand; C. Indirect route: license or partner with an existing home-appliance maker so RATIONAL's technology reaches home users without its own consumer retail; D. Adjacent customer group not suggested by the question: small professional or prosumer users (bakeries, caterers, serious home bakers, small restaurants) using a scaled-down version; E. Existing consumer footprint: check whether RATIONAL already sells to individuals through a shop, accessories, cookbooks, or online, and grow that before any new product; F. Technology licensing or component sale (e.g. steam or cooking-control modules) without any RATIONAL-branded consumer product.
Searched for "RATIONAL consumer home cooking products individual buyers"; found rational-anova-oven, rational-ir-customers, rational-ir-leader.

T1: Serious home cooks would pay a premium for a compact, RATIONAL-branded combi-steamer because it gives professional steam results at home, so a maker that carries its commercial technology and brand into a small appliance could capture a premium price in a niche consumer segment. Who benefits: Affluent home cooks and enthusiasts who already want steam or combi results; RATIONAL, which would earn premium margins and a consumer brand from existing engineering.. Why behaviour changes: Home cooks buy appliances as status and capability signals. A professional brand's name and proven steam performance would make a home unit feel like a serious upgrade over generic countertop ovens, which changes purchase choice from price to brand credibility.. How value is captured: Priced above mainstream countertop combi ovens, sold through premium retail or direct online, with the commercial brand and existing steam engineering as the moat; margin comes from a smaller product sold at a premium, not from the professional channel.. Assumptions: Home buyers value professional-brand credibility enough to pay a clear premium; A compact unit can be built on existing technology at acceptable cost; Premium home appliance retail and online channels are reachable without the commercial sales force; RATIONAL's brand has enough recognition among consumers, not only chefs. Predictions: Stated willingness to pay for a branded compact unit is materially above that for an unbranded equivalent in a survey of home cooks; Pre-orders or waitlist sign-ups for a prototype concentrate in users who already own a countertop combi or steam oven; Conversion falls sharply when the price passes the level of established premium home combi ovens.

T2: Home buyers do not value professional throughput or service, so a shrunken commercial combi-steamer would not win on its own; the commercially valuable asset is the professional service network and software ecosystem. RATIONAL would capture value by licensing its steam and cooking-control technology to an established home-appliance maker, which already has consumer retail, rather than selling a RATIONAL-branded product itself. Who benefits: Established home-appliance makers, who gain proven steam technology without R&D cost; RATIONAL, which earns licence fees and avoids consumer marketing, returns and retail risk.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers buy home appliances through trusted retail brands with service networks already in place. A licensed component inside a known brand reaches buyers who would not seek out a professional brand, and the licensor avoids the cost of building a consumer brand from scratch.. How value is captured: Per-unit royalty or component sale to a licensee, with the licensee carrying consumer marketing, distribution and warranty. RATIONAL's margin depends on licence terms and volume, not on consumer price.. Assumptions: A home-appliance partner would pay a royalty for steam or control technology; Consumers do not need the RATIONAL name to value steam performance; Licensing does not cannibalise the professional business or leak core know-how; Partner distribution reaches enough home buyers to justify royalties. Predictions: Appliance makers that already sell countertop steam or combi ovens would accept licence terms when offered a component pilot; Consumer tests of an unbranded steam-combi unit match the performance perception of a RATIONAL-branded unit, showing little brand premium; Royalty revenue stays small relative to professional sales unless a partner achieves high volume.

T1 supports, from rational-anova-oven (market_fact): "the Anova Precision Oven, a countertop combi oven that supported both steam and convection cooking methods and could be used either alongside other Precision Cooker products or by itself.". Does not show: Whether home buyers would pay a premium for a RATIONAL-branded unit, whether Anova sells well, or whether a brand name adds value. It shows only that a home countertop combi oven is sold by another company, so a home market for such products exists in at least one case. It is a Wikipedia summary with an unknown date and no sales data..

T2 neutral, from rational-ir-customers (company_assertion): "The customer base ranges from restaurants and hotels, company canteens, hospitals, schools, universities, the military, prisons and retirement homes to fast-food restaurants, party services, supermarkets, bakeries and snack bars, butchers, petrol stations and delivery services, including so-called ghost kitchens.". Does not show: Whether the commercial service network or software is what customers pay for, whether home buyers lack interest in it, or whether any licensing deal exists. The list describes who buys commercially; it does not show which asset earns the margin, and home buyers are not on it..
Looked for evidence against T1: "countertop combi oven home market failure returns low sales premium brand not valued"; found rational-anova-oven, rational-combi-countertop, rational-wiki-icombi90.

T1 contradicts, from rational-combi-countertop (market_fact): "These countertop appliances have the same characteristic changes as the full-size household appliances, except that they are smaller, and cost significantly less than a full-size oven.". Does not show: Whether home buyers would pay a premium for a RATIONAL-branded unit, what the price level of countertop combi ovens is in any market, or whether premium units sell. This is a Wikipedia summary with unknown geography and date. It weakens the premise that a compact combi must be priced above mainstream units, but it does not show that premium pricing fails..

Test "Brand-premium and licence-interest test for a compact steam-combi concept" between T1; T2. Method: Two parallel low-cost arms. (a) Online concept test: a landing page describing a compact steam-combi for home use, shown at three price points (proposed: mid, premium, high relative to established countertop combi ovens) with and without the RATIONAL name on the page, randomised between visitors. Measure waitlist sign-ups with a deposit-free email. (b) Outreach to 8 to 10 home-appliance makers that already sell countertop steam or combi ovens, asking whether they would evaluate a licensed steam-control component, measured by meetings and written interest.. Sample: Arm (a): proposed 1,500 to 2,000 home-cook visitors recruited through paid online ads targeted to people who own or research countertop ovens, in one European market. Arm (b): 8 to 10 appliance makers (proposed).. Measure: Arm (a): waitlist conversion rate by price point and by brand condition, with the gap between branded and unbranded pages. Arm (b): number of makers agreeing to a substantive call and written interest in a licence pilot.. Predictions: T1: Conversion at the premium price is at least as high on the RATIONAL-branded page as on the unbranded page, and the branded page keeps meaningful conversion at a price above mainstream countertop units. Appliance makers show little interest in licensing because they expect to build their own steam technology.; T2: The brand condition makes little difference to conversion, because buyers respond to price and function, not the professional name. Several appliance makers agree to evaluate a licensed component, and interest is strongest in licence terms rather than product design.. Decision rule: Favour T1 (proposed product) only if the branded premium-price arm converts at least 1.5 times the unbranded premium-price arm AND the branded premium-price conversion is at least 2% of visitors, AND fewer than 3 of the appliance makers agree to a substantive licensing discussion. Favour T2 (licensing) if the brand gap is below 1.2 times AND at least 3 appliance makers agree to a substantive call. Otherwise, neither is supported; do not proceed to a product or licence and seek a sales-data source. All thresholds are analyst proposals, not established benchmarks.. Cost: 12000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not commit to a RATIONAL-branded home product or a licence yet. Keep professional kitchens as the core, and run the proposed X1 test to decide between a branded compact unit (T1) and licensing (T2). The evidence I have read does not settle either. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: SYN-D is a SIMULATED warehouse label-printer test that measures nothing about home cooks, buyers or premium pricing, so it bears on neither theory and I do not count it. T1 stays as it was, uncertain, resting on the real evidence I have read. New claim: none. Evidence: rational-anova-oven; rational-combi-countertop.

T2 kept: Supposing SYN-D were real: a label printer that slightly cuts warehouse packing errors would say nothing about whether home buyers value professional throughput or service, or whether appliance makers would license steam control. It would not change T2 in either direction. It is SIMULATED and is not counted in the investigation's evidence. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Do not build a RATIONAL-branded home product or sign a licence yet. Keep professional kitchens as the core, and run test X1 (proposed, not run, 12,000 EUR, 8 weeks) to decide between a branded compact home unit (T1) and licensing steam technology to an existing home-appliance maker (T2). The public evidence I read does not establish demand from home cooks for a RATIONAL product, nor a licensing market. Target customer: Serious home cooks who already own a countertop combi or steam oven and research upgrades. This is a hypothesis under test, not a finding.. Value proposition: A compact steam-combi carrying professional steam performance and the RATIONAL name, priced above mainstream countertop units. Untested: the premium is what X1 would measure.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run X1: branded versus unbranded landing page at three price points, plus outreach to 8 to 10 home-appliance makers, and apply the decision rule as written. Before running it, check RATIONAL's annual reports for any consumer or accessories revenue. I did not search for these.. Uncertainty: High. I read three company pages and two Wikipedia summaries, with unknown dates and no sales data. I found no evidence that RATIONAL sells to individual buyers, but I did not verify this against its financial reports, and I did not reconcile any financial data. The Anova item shows a home combi oven exists from another company, not that a RATIONAL one would sell. The countertop item says such units cost much less than full-size ovens, which weakens the premium premise. Neither theory has direct support. The simulated warehouse result (SYN-D) was excluded.. Would change if: Test X1 shows the branded premium-price page converts less than 1.5 times the unbranded one, or below 2% of visitors, which favours neither a product nor a licence; At least 3 appliance makers take a substantive licensing call, which would favour T2 over a branded product; RATIONAL's annual reports show existing consumer or accessories revenue that shows willingness to pay for its name at home; Credible sales data for premium countertop combi ovens showing premium-brand units sell well, or sell poorly; Evidence that RATIONAL's engineering cannot be scaled down without losing the performance that justifies a premium. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

events.text: Objective: Decide whether Aquaporin should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its existing B2B water-membrane offering, and identify what evidence would justify that investment. Do not assume the company's intentions.. Constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only; company has not asked this question and nothing here describes its intentions; Financial data may be incomplete; state what could not be found; Test budget of EUR 20000 and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions, not company figures; Search budget is limited; challenge_theory allowance is one; do not cite SIMULATED results; Must first establish how far Aquaporin already reaches individual buyers; Recommendation must be framed as a hypothesis test, not as advice on what the company should do. Alternatives: No expansion: remain a B2B membrane supplier and license technology to existing partners; Product redesign: consumer-branded point-of-use drinking-water purifier or replacement cartridge using Aquaporin membranes, sold direct to households; Different route to buyers: partner or white-label with established consumer water-filter or appliance brands, with recurring cartridge sales; Different customer group: institutional or commercial buyers such as offices, hospitality, schools or healthcare, using a packaged point-of-use product; Specific use case: travel, emergency or off-grid water purification for a niche segment; Technology licensing to desalination or industrial water-treatment customers rather than consumers.
Searched for "Aquaporin consumer water purifier"; found aqp-one-purifier-2021, aqp-philips-china-supply-2023, aqp-vestel-rafine-pro-2024.

T1: Consumers in the drinking-water purifier market buy on the appliance brand's trust and channel, so an ingredient membrane brand only earns a premium when a large partner brand co-markets it. Aquaporin's consumer value therefore comes mainly from ingredient-brand supply deals, and the premium is shared with the partner. Who benefits: Appliance brands (Philips, Vestel) that gain a technology story and retail reach; Aquaporin, which earns supply margin and royalty-like volume without owning retail.. Why behaviour changes: Households trust a known appliance brand for safety and filtration claims they cannot verify, and a recognised membrane name adds credibility on top of that trust. The partner's shelf, service network and warranty make the purchase feel safe.. How value is captured: Exclusive or regional supply agreements for membranes or cartridges sold into partner-branded devices, with recurring consumable revenue tied to partner installed base.. Assumptions: Consumers recognise and value the ingredient brand in partner marketing; Partner brands are willing to pay for exclusivity; Replacement cartridge volumes follow the partner's installed base. Predictions: Partner-branded products with the ingredient logo sell at a higher price or faster rate than equivalent products without it, in matched channels; Sales growth in partner markets tracks the partner's distribution rather than Aquaporin's own marketing; Aquaporin's consumer revenue is concentrated in a few partner contracts.

T2: Consumers treat drinking-water purification as a recurring, low-attention chore, so the decisive value is the replacement cartridge schedule and convenience of reordering. A company that controls a cartridge subscription can capture most lifetime value even if the device is sold cheaply or by others. Who benefits: Aquaporin, if it owns the replacement-cartridge relationship; households, which gain automatic reminders and fewer missed changes.. Why behaviour changes: Households rarely think about filters until taste or a warning appears, and they often keep using expired cartridges. A simple reorder or subscription changes that habit and locks in repeat purchase.. How value is captured: Recurring sales of membrane cartridges via direct subscription or retail reorder, priced above a commodity filter's cost per litre.. Assumptions: Cartridge replacement is a meaningful share of lifetime revenue; Consumers will reorder through a branded channel rather than buy generic cartridges; A proprietary or certified cartridge can be enforced without legal or compatibility barriers. Predictions: Households on a reminder or subscription replace cartridges on schedule more often than households without one; Price premium for the membrane cartridge holds only where cartridge compatibility is controlled; Share of lifetime value from cartridges exceeds device margin in partner channels.

T1 supports, from aqp-philips-china-supply-2023 (company_assertion): "Signed an exclusive supply agreement with AquaShield, the global brand partner of Philips Water Solutions for supply of membrane to all Philips-branded purifiers in China, with a doubling of sales compared to 2022". Does not show: Shows that a partner-brand supply deal exists and that Aquaporin reports growth from it. It does not show that consumers pay more or buy faster because the Aquaporin membrane is named, nor how much of the growth is the Philips brand rather than the membrane. The figure is the company's own report, not audited or independent..

T2 supports, from aqp-one-purifier-2021 (company_assertion): "ONE’s only maintenance requirement is cartridge replacement which can easily be done by oneself.". Does not show: Shows the company designs its own device around cartridge replacement and describes it as the only upkeep. It does not show that households reorder cartridges on schedule, that a reminder changes behaviour, or that cartridge revenue exceeds device margin. The claim is the company's own product description, and the product is sold through distributors in several countries..

Looked for evidence against T1: "ingredient brand consumer premium water purifier partner brand Aquaporin Inside sales price"; found aqp-philips-china-supply-2023, aqp-vestel-rafine-pro-2024, aqp-strategic-review-failed.

Declined to test: The company's announcement (No. 04/2026, dated 2026-01-30, third-party copy) says it withdrew its offering and resolved to start insolvency proceedings after failing to find funding or partners. A 20000 EUR, 12-week consumer test would answer a question no current owner can act on, since there is no funded team for a new consumer proposition. The theories stay untested, but the investment question is settled by the insolvency.

Favours T1: Do not pursue a differentiated consumer proposition for Aquaporin. The company announced withdrawal of its offering and insolvency proceedings (Company announcement No. 04/2026, dated 2026-01-30, third-party copy). A consumer investment cannot be funded by the current company, so the question of what evidence would justify it has no actionable owner here. If the technology is acquired, the relevant question becomes whether an acquirer can earn a premium through ingredient-brand partnerships, which T1 addresses. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: SYN-D is a SIMULATED warehouse label-printer test that measured nothing about buyers or wearers, so it bears on neither T1 nor T2. It changes nothing. T1 stays an untested hypothesis, and the company's insolvency removes any owner for acting on it. I cite no SIMULATED result. New claim: none. Evidence: aqp-philips-china-supply-2023.

T2 kept: SYN-D is a SIMULATED warehouse label-printer test that measured nothing about cartridge reorders or households, so even if it were real it would bear on neither theory. Nothing changes. T2 stays untested, and I rely on no simulated result. New claim: none. Evidence: aqp-one-purifier-2021.

T1 kept: Supposing SYN-D were real: it reports a warehouse label printer reducing packing errors and measures nothing about buyers, wearers or brand premiums. It bears on T1 only by absence, so T1 is unchanged. I do not cite it as evidence. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for Aquaporin now. The company's own announcement (No. 04/2026, dated 2026-01-30, third-party copy on Bolsamania) says it withdrew its offering and resolved to start insolvency proceedings after failing to find investors or partners to fund commercialisation. Without a funded owner, no consumer test or investment decision can be acted on. If the technology or partner contracts are acquired, the question becomes whether an acquirer could earn a premium through ingredient-brand partnerships, which is the open question T1 addresses. Target customer: None for Aquaporin at present. The consumer groups its existing deals reach are households in partner markets: Philips purifiers in China and Vestel Rafine PRO in Turkey, plus the company's own ONE purifier distributed in several regions.. Value proposition: Ingredient-brand membrane supply to appliance partners, with recurring cartridge revenue. Untested; all evidence is company-reported.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Verify the insolvency status from the original Danish announcement or the court or company registry, which I have not checked. If the technology or partner contracts are for sale, check whether any buyer has a funded consumer plan before designing any test.. Uncertainty: I could not find audited financials, sales by channel, or independent data on consumer willingness to pay for an ingredient brand. The Philips and Vestel evidence is company-reported and does not separate brand premium from the appliance brand's own pull. T2 (cartridge recurrence) rests on a product description with no reorder data. The challenge search found no evidence against T1, only company claims and the insolvency notice. I did not cite the simulated result, which measured nothing relevant.. Would change if: The original announcement or a registry record shows the insolvency was withdrawn, or the company was refinanced with a funded consumer plan; A named acquirer of the technology or partner contracts states a consumer product plan with budget; Independent or audited data show partner-branded purifiers with the membrane logo selling at a measurable premium over matched products without it; Reorder or subscription data show cartridge replacement is a large share of partner-channel revenue. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.
