events.text: Objective: Decide whether RATIONAL AG should build a differentiated proposition for home cooks using its commercial combi-steamer technology, or keep its focus on professional kitchens, and identify what evidence would justify either choice. Judge from public sources only, without assuming what the company already sells to individual buyers.. Constraints: Outside analyst working only from public sources; no contact with the company and no knowledge of its intentions; Test budget EUR 20,000 and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions, not company figures; Search budget of 7 searches remaining; each theory needs a distinct causal mechanism; Partly public financial data: report what cannot be found or reconcile rather than filling gaps; Every observed number must come from a source read; proposed or estimated numbers must be labelled; SIMULATED results are not evidence and will not be cited. Alternatives: A. No expansion: stay with professional kitchens and deepen the commercial core (service, software, installed-base upgrades, aftermarket and accessories for existing commercial owners); B. Consumer-facing flagship: a premium home-sized combi-steamer sold direct to affluent home cooks under the RATIONAL brand; C. Indirect route: license or co-brand the technology to existing home-appliance makers rather than selling under the RATIONAL brand; D. Prosumer and small-operator segment: serious amateurs, small restaurants, caterers and food-service start-ups, served with smaller or lower-cost units, without a full home product; E. Commercial redesign as growth route: lower-skill operation, small kitchens and institutional catering before any consumer move; F. Partner-led test: sell through premium kitchen retailers or cooking-school channels to test consumer demand without building a consumer organisation.
Searched for "RATIONAL combi-steamer home cooks consumer"; found rational-combi-makers, rational-ir-potential, rational-wiki-1978.
Searched for "RATIONAL home appliances consumer sales individual buyers"; found rational-wiki-icombi90, rational-anova-electrolux, rational-ir-customers.

T1: Home cooks who already cook seriously would pay a premium for a home-sized combi-steamer built on commercial-grade engineering, because the value they want (repeatable results, time saved, low-fat cooking) is a performance benefit, not a fashion or design benefit. RATIONAL could capture that premium by selling a direct, premium-priced unit. Who benefits: Affluent serious home cooks who value repeatable results and are willing to buy a premium appliance; RATIONAL, through a higher-margin direct product line.. Why behaviour changes: A home cook who already invests in cookware and knives sees a commercial-grade appliance as a status-consistent upgrade. The commercial pedigree signals performance, so they buy a product they would not buy from a standard home brand.. How value is captured: RATIONAL sells a premium home unit under its own brand, direct or through premium retail, and earns a price premium over mainstream home steam ovens, using its existing engineering and brand.. Assumptions: Home buyers will pay a price premium for commercial-grade performance over incumbent home products (Miele, Bosch, AEG, Gaggenau); Kitchen space and installation are not decisive barriers for the target buyer; Demand is concentrated in a small affluent segment large enough to repay development cost. Predictions: Stated willingness to pay for a commercial-grade home unit is higher among buyers who already own premium cookware than among general home buyers; Conversion from a demo or sample at a premium retailer is higher where the commercial pedigree is shown than where it is hidden; Buyers cite performance or results rather than design when asked why they chose the unit.

T2: Home combi-steamers are bought as part of a kitchen renovation, not as standalone appliances. Buyers choose built-in units through their kitchen designer or installer, so a brand's chance depends on its relationship with that installation channel, and the value goes to whoever owns that channel, usually through licensing rather than a RATIONAL-branded product. Who benefits: Kitchen-furniture and appliance makers that already own the installer and designer channel (incumbents such as Miele, Bosch, AEG, Gaggenau); RATIONAL only if it licenses its technology to them.. Why behaviour changes: A home buyer doing a kitchen refit accepts the designer's built-in recommendation and the brand that fits the cabinetry. Standalone purchase by a home cook is rare, so the choice of appliance follows the kitchen plan, not the cooking enthusiasm.. How value is captured: RATIONAL licenses the combi-steamer technology to an existing home-appliance maker, earning royalties, and avoids building a consumer brand, sales force or service network.. Assumptions: Home combi-steamers are mostly bought as built-in units during kitchen renovations, not as standalone purchases; Incumbent appliance makers already hold the installer and designer relationships that decide the brand; A licensee would accept RATIONAL technology and share margin. Predictions: Share of home combi-steamer sales made through kitchen-installer channels is higher than through general retail; Brands with strong kitchen-designer relationships hold a larger share of built-in combi-steamer sales than brands with only retail presence; Buyers asked where they chose the unit say the kitchen designer or installer recommended it.

T1 neutral, from rational-ir-potential (company_assertion): "According to company estimates, the global market potential for combi-steamers is 4.8 million customers, around 75% of whom still use traditional cooking appliances.". Does not show: It gives no split between professional and home customers, so it cannot show how many home cooks would pay a premium for a commercial-grade unit. It is the company's own estimate of market potential, not a measured demand figure, and it does not say whether the 4.8 million are commercial or domestic..

T1 supports, from rational-anova-electrolux (analogy): "On February 6, 2017, Anova was acquired by Electrolux , a home appliance company, for a total of US$250 million.". Does not show: Anova sells sous-vide circulators, not combi-steamers, and the acquisition price does not show what a premium home buyer pays for commercial-grade engineering. It shows only that a home appliance maker valued a serious-home-cooking product line, which is an analogy for T1's demand, not proof of it..

T2 supports, from rational-combi-makers (market_fact): "Germany: RATIONAL AG , Gaggenau Hausgeräte , PALUX, Convotherm, MKN, ELOMA, Miele , AEG (part of Electrolux), Bosch.". Does not show: This is a list of German combi-steamer makers, not a share of sales or a channel breakdown. It shows that home-appliance makers (Gaggenau Hausgeräte, Miele, AEG, Bosch) are in the category, but not that they hold the installer or designer relationships that decide brand choice, and not how home units are sold..

Looked for evidence against T1: "home buyers premium price commercial-grade appliance willingness to pay consumer combi steamer"; found rational-combi-history, rational-combi-countertop, rational-ir-potential.

T1 contradicts, from rational-combi-countertop (market_fact): "These countertop appliances have the same characteristic changes as the full-size household appliances, except that they are smaller, and cost significantly less than a full-size oven.". Does not show: The excerpt gives no prices, no buyer data and no geography, so it cannot show how large the price gap is or whether any home buyer pays a premium for commercial pedigree. It contradicts only the assumption that home units are sold at a premium over mainstream home ovens; it does not show that commercial-grade buyers would reject a premium unit..

Test "Premium-pedigree conjoint and channel-intercept test (proposed)" between T1; T2. Method: Two-part test. (a) Online choice-based conjoint with a priced concept card for a countertop combi-steamer, varying brand pedigree (commercial-kitchen heritage vs none), price tier and where it is bought (direct/premium retail vs kitchen-installer/designer recommendation). (b) Intercept interviews at 2-3 premium kitchen showrooms, asking who influenced the choice of any built-in or countertop oven in the last kitchen refit.. Sample: Proposed: 300 online panel respondents who cook at home at least 3 times a week and own premium cookware, plus 60 showroom intercepts across 2-3 showrooms in one German city. Estimated cost EUR 12,000-15,000 for panel and fieldwork.. Measure: (a) Share of choices that pay the premium tier for the commercial-pedigree brand over the same spec without pedigree; part-worth utility of brand pedigree vs installer recommendation. (b) Share of recent oven buyers who say the designer or installer chose the appliance.. Predictions: T1: Premium-tier share for the commercial-pedigree brand is clearly above zero among serious cooks, and pedigree utility exceeds the installer-recommendation utility; most showroom buyers chose their own appliance, not the installer.; T2: Installer or designer influence dominates choice (installer-recommendation utility larger than pedigree utility), and most showroom buyers say the installer or designer chose the appliance; pedigree has little weight once channel is held constant.. Decision rule: Favour T1 if pedigree part-worth is positive and significant at the 95% level AND fewer than 40% of showroom buyers say an installer or designer chose the appliance. Favour T2 if installer or designer influence is at least 60% of showroom buyers OR installer-recommendation part-worth exceeds pedigree part-worth. Otherwise treat both as unresolved and do not commit to a home product.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not commit to a RATIONAL-branded home product yet. Run the proposed low-cost test. Keep the professional business as the core, and treat home expansion as an option to be tested, not a decision. Public sources so far show no evidence that RATIONAL sells to individual buyers, and the evidence on whether home cooks would pay a premium is absent. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Do not commit to a RATIONAL-branded home combi-steamer now. Keep professional kitchens as the core. Run the proposed low-cost conjoint and showroom test (about EUR 18,000 and 10 weeks; both figures are my estimates) before deciding on any home product. Target customer: Serious home cooks who already invest in premium cookware and cook several times a week (hypothesis to test, not a finding).. Value proposition: Commercial-grade performance and repeatability in a home unit, priced above mainstream home ovens. This is hypothesis T1 only; the premium premise is contradicted for the home category as a whole and must be tested.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run test X1. First check RATIONAL's annual report for any home or consumer segment, since I could not find or reconcile the financial split between commercial and any consumer sales.. Uncertainty: High. No source shows RATIONAL sells to individual buyers. The 4.8 million market figure is a company estimate with no professional/home split. Incumbents (Miele, Bosch, AEG, Gaggenau Hausgeräte) are in home combi-steamers, described as cheaper than full-size ovens. I read no financial statements. Anova is an analogy for a different product. No real test has been run.. Would change if: Conjoint shows no positive pedigree part-worth among serious home cooks (rejects T1); Showroom buyers say an installer or designer chose the appliance in 60% or more of cases (favours T2 and licensing); Filings show RATIONAL already sells a premium consumer line; Evidence that home combi-steamer prices sit at commercial-grade levels (supports T1); Independent data on home-cook demand size. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

case.question: Should Electrolux Professional Group develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing professional laundry offering? What evidence would justify that investment?
case.source_limits: Evidence is limited to the case dossier: each source shows everything the dossier holds for it, often a short excerpt, not the whole original. Results marked simulated are what-if evidence, not real observations.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 household washing-machine buyers eligible for the same professional-derived washer offer were assigned equally to two descriptions. Both descriptions showed the same machine, brand, price, warranty, availability, service terms and verified specifications. One emphasized durability and repairability; the other emphasized washing performance and the upfront price. No discount or extra service was added. The outcome was a paid, refundable purchase reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned buyers per arm. There were 32 reservations in the durability-and-repairability description arm and 72 in the performance-and-price description arm. This tests the incremental effect of the description in this recruited population, not actual appliance lifetime, delivery capability, market size, profitability or sustained repurchase. A weaker result would not refute a different channel or product theory.

In addition, residential customers are increasingly demanding commercial-quality products for the home, and our machines represent a compelling fit for this select but growing segment of the residential market.
Consumer‑operated setups enable residents, guests or members to run their own laundry in multi‑family buildings, student housing, campsites, marinas, gyms or staff facilities.

Electrolux Professional provides integrated solutions designed for different formats – laundromats, bungalows and consumer‑operated – combining reliability, resource efficiency and serviceability to maximize uptime and ROI.

events.text: Objective: Decide whether Electrolux Professional Group should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for one specific use case beyond its professional laundry offering, and identify what evidence would justify that investment.. Constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only, with no company contact or assumed intentions; Financial and contractual detail may be non-public, so gaps must be stated; Test budget of 20000 EUR and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions; 7 searches remain, so evidence gathering must be targeted; First establish how far EPG already reaches individual buyers rather than assuming it does not. Alternatives: No expansion: stay purely professional in commercial laundry and food-service; Product redesign: adapt an existing professional machine, such as a compact or lower-capacity model, for home or small-household use under the same brand; Different route to buyers: sell existing or adapted products to consumers through retail, e-commerce or partner channels; Different customer group: target small commercial users such as small hospitality operators, cafes or short-let properties as a middle tier; Service model: offer laundry-as-a-service or equipment-as-a-service to individuals or small operators, earning on maintenance and consumables; Adjacent category: enter a consumer category for prosumers, such as dishwashing or cooking, using food-service know-how.
Searched for "Electrolux Professional consumer products home laundry"; found epro-consumer-operated, epro-selfservice-formats, epro-alliance-residential-segment.

T1: Households that want commercial-grade durability will buy a compact professional-grade washer for the home at a premium, so a maker with existing commercial engineering can earn a price premium on a consumer line. Who benefits: Households who replace machines often and value durability and repairability, and the maker, which can reuse commercial designs.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers who have been frustrated by short-lived appliances may pay more for a machine that is built to last, once they see it as a long-term purchase rather than a disposable one.. How value is captured: Premium unit pricing and replacement parts or service sold direct or through retail partners, with margin above the mass-market appliance segment.. Assumptions: A meaningful share of households will pay a premium for durability over features; Commercial-grade machines can meet home space, noise and power constraints at acceptable cost; Existing retail or partner channels can reach these buyers without a large new sales force. Predictions: Stated willingness to pay a durability premium is high among households that report recent appliance failure; Conversion to purchase falls sharply when price exceeds the mass-market premium band; Buyers cite longevity and repairability more than brand or features in survey responses.

T2: The buyer that matters is the small property operator, not the household. Landlords and small operators will buy a self-service laundry setup for residents or guests because it adds rental income with little staffing, so a maker that already sells to these operators can capture value through equipment, service and consumables without any direct-to-consumer sale. Who benefits: Property owners, campsite and marina operators, and student housing managers, who gain an amenity that earns revenue or retains tenants; and the maker, which sells equipment plus a service and consumables stream.. Why behaviour changes: Operators switch to paying for a self-service laundry when the equipment is reliable and low-maintenance enough that they do not need staff, and when the income from pay-per-use exceeds the cost of the machines.. How value is captured: Equipment sales to operators, followed by recurring service contracts, spare parts and consumables tied to machine uptime.. Assumptions: Operators value uptime and low serviceability cost more than upfront price; Residents or guests will pay per use for an on-site machine; The existing self-service format already reaches these operators, so the gap is in a specific use case rather than the whole consumer market. Predictions: Operators who already run self-service laundry report uptime and service response as their top purchase criteria; Installed self-service sites show a steady stream of service and consumables revenue per machine; Demand is concentrated in property types with on-site laundry need, not in single-household purchases.

T1 supports, from epro-alliance-residential-segment (company_assertion): "residential customers are increasingly demanding commercial-quality products for the home, and our machines represent a compelling fit for this select but growing segment of the residential market.". Does not show: This is a competitor's (Alliance Laundry) prospectus claim about its own products, not EPG and not independent data. It does not show household willingness to pay a premium, the size of the segment, or any purchase conversion. The word 'select' suggests a niche..

T2 supports, from epro-consumer-operated (company_assertion): "Consumer‑operated setups enable residents, guests or members to run their own laundry in multi‑family buildings, student housing, campsites, marinas, gyms or staff facilities.". Does not show: This is EPG's own product-page description of a use case. It shows the offering exists, not that operators buy it, that sites earn enough to justify it, or that service and consumables revenue follows. It is not uptake data..

Looked for evidence against T2: "self-service laundry operators decline closures low utilisation laundromat market downturn"; found epro-selfservice-formats, epro-consumer-operated, epro-alliance-residential-segment.

Test "Operator pilot: pay-per-use self-service setup with service contract" between T1; T2. Method: Recruit small property operators (student housing, campsites, small multi-family buildings) and offer a priced self-service laundry setup with a bundled service contract. Measure whether they sign a letter of intent. In parallel, run a short household survey using a durability-premium price test to see whether consumers would pay a premium for a compact commercial-grade machine.. Sample: Proposed: 15 small operators and about 300 households in 2 regions. Sample sizes are analyst estimates, not company figures.. Measure: Operators: signed letter of intent with a service contract, and stated uptime requirements. Households: share willing to pay at the proposed premium price versus the mass-market price band.. Predictions: T1: Households report high willingness to pay a durability premium, and the premium-price acceptance rate stays high across the price range tested. Operators show low interest in a service contract.; T2: Operators sign letters of intent at a meaningful rate, prioritise uptime and service response, and accept a recurring service fee. Household premium acceptance is weak or falls sharply at the premium price.. Decision rule: Proposed threshold: pursue the operator-focused proposition if at least 4 of 15 operators (about 25%) sign a letter of intent that includes a recurring service contract, and household premium acceptance is below the level needed to support a direct-to-consumer line. If fewer than 2 of 15 sign, drop the proposition and keep EPG professional-only. Between these, extend the test rather than decide.. Cost: 14000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T2: Do not commit to a consumer line yet. Favour the operator route first: test whether small property operators will buy a priced self-service setup with a service contract, through the existing self-service offering. Keep EPG professional-only until the pilot reports. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1 revised: Treating SYN-EPRO-UPDATE as a what-if: a durability-and-repairability description produced 32 uncancelled reservations out of 400 buyers (8%), against 72 out of 400 (18%) for a performance-and-price description, with the same machine, price and terms. If real, this would weaken the claim that households pay a premium for durability framing. It tests only a description effect in one recruited population, not appliance lifetime, market size, or operator demand, so it does not refute the idea that a commercial-grade machine could sell to some households. The revised claim is narrower. New claim: A compact commercial-grade washer may sell to some households, but in this what-if a durability description did not beat a performance and price description, so a durability premium cannot be assumed.. Evidence: SYN-EPRO-UPDATE.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a consumer product line now. Test the operator route first. EPG already sells self-service laundry setups to operators and property owners (its own product page lists multi-family buildings, student housing, campsites, marinas, gyms and staff facilities). Run a small priced pilot to see whether those operators will commit to equipment plus a recurring service contract. Keep EPG professional-only until the pilot reports. Target customer: Small property operators, such as student housing managers, campsite and marina operators, and small multi-family landlords, who want on-site laundry for residents or guests without staff.. Value proposition: A self-service laundry setup from EPG's existing format range, bundled with reliability and serviceability to protect uptime, with revenue from equipment, service and consumables.. Favoured theory: T2. Next action: Run the operator pilot X1 (proposed: 15 operators, about 14,000 EUR, 10 weeks; all figures analyst estimates). Proceed only if at least 4 of 15 sign a letter of intent that includes a recurring service contract. Drop the proposition if fewer than 2 do. Extend the test between those.. Uncertainty: Large. The only evidence I read is EPG's own product pages and a competitor's (Alliance Laundry) IPO profile on North American residential demand. None reports sales, uptake, prices, margins or service revenue. The challenge search for evidence against T2 returned only the same pages, so T2 was not tested against outside data. EPG's financial, contract and channel detail is not public to me. The T1 durability idea rests on one competitor claim with no willingness-to-pay data.. Would change if: Pilot operators decline service contracts or cite only upfront price, which would weaken T2; Public EPG or peer data shows operator self-service revenue is flat or falling; Independent household data showed a durability premium large enough to support a direct-to-consumer line; EPG disclosed existing consumer sales or customer data showing real uptake; Evidence showed a competitor dominates small-operator self-service with lower-cost service. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

case.question: Should RATIONAL develop a differentiated proposition for home cooks, building on its commercial combi-steamer technology, or stay with professional kitchens? What evidence would justify either choice?
case.source_limits: Evidence is limited to the case dossier: each source shows everything the dossier holds for it, often a short excerpt, not the whole original. Results marked simulated are what-if evidence, not real observations.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 72 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 32 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.

Subsequent products included the Anova Precision Cooker Nano and the Anova Precision Oven, a countertop combi oven that supported both steam and convection cooking methods and could be used either alongside other Precision Cooker products or by itself.
In addition to the professional food-service models, there are also smaller combi steamers for private household use.

The customer base ranges from restaurants and hotels, company canteens, hospitals, schools, universities, the military, prisons and retirement homes to fast-food restaurants, party services, supermarkets, bakeries and snack bars, butchers, petrol stations and delivery services, including so-called ghost kitchens.
Combi ovens (iCombi product line) generate approximately 90% of Rational's appliance sales, while about 10% comes from the iVario series and newly added iHexagon appliances.

events.text: Objective: Decide whether RATIONAL AG should build a differentiated proposition for home cooks using its commercial combi-steamer technology, or keep its focus on professional kitchens, and identify what evidence would justify each choice.. Constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only; no contact with the company and no knowledge of its intentions; Test budget 20000 EUR and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions, not company figures; Company financial data is partly public; must state what could not be found or reconciled; Must establish first what RATIONAL already sells to individual buyers rather than assume; Search budget of 8 searches, 7 remaining after the brief. Alternatives: No expansion: remain purely professional-kitchen focused; Consumer product redesign: a scaled-down or re-engineered combi-steamer for home kitchens sold directly; Different route to buyers: sell existing or adapted products to home cooks via retail, partners or online without redesign; Different customer group: target small professional or semi-professional users (cafes, caterers, serious home-cook enthusiasts) rather than mass home cooks; Licensing or component supply of steam-cooking technology to appliance makers who own the home brand; Service and recipe/software layer around existing professional units, sold to professional customers or prosumers.
Searched for "RATIONAL home consumer products iCombi home cooking"; found rational-wiki-icombi90, rational-anova-oven, rational-ir-customers.

T1: Serious home cooks will pay a premium for a professional-grade steam combi oven if it is sold as a prosumer appliance with a recipe layer, so RATIONAL could earn margin by selling a scaled-down iCombi directly to this group. Who benefits: RATIONAL, through a premium-priced consumer or prosumer unit, and enthusiast home cooks who value precision and results.. Why behaviour changes: Home cooks already buy countertop combi ovens (Anova Precision Oven) and treat steam cooking as a quality marker, so a brand with professional credibility can command a price above mass-market units.. How value is captured: Direct sales or premium retail margin on a higher-priced appliance, plus accessories, recipes and software subscriptions that the manufacturer controls.. Assumptions: A meaningful number of home buyers will pay several times the price of mainstream countertop ovens; Professional-grade build and footprint can be made to fit home kitchens and home power supply at acceptable cost; Brand credibility from commercial kitchens transfers to home buyers; Sales and service through retail or online can be run without eroding the professional channel. Predictions: Purchase intent among enthusiast home cooks at the target price exceeds a set threshold in a stated-preference or pre-order test; Buyers of an existing premium countertop combi oven show high willingness to pay for steam-specific features; Accessory and recipe revenue per unit is non-trivial relative to hardware margin.

T2: RATIONAL's value comes from commercial labour, food-cost and throughput savings that depend on professional kitchen workflows, so home buyers lack the economic reason to pay for the system and the professional focus earns more. Who benefits: Professional kitchen operators (restaurants, canteens, hospitals) who buy for measurable labour and yield gains, and RATIONAL, which keeps its service and installation network.. Why behaviour changes: Commercial buyers switch to combi-steamers because they cut cooking time, staff and waste across many meals a day; home cooks cook a few meals a week and do not gain the same return, so the purchase rationale does not transfer.. How value is captured: Equipment sales plus installation, service contracts, cleaning systems and consumables, all tied to professional throughput and uptime.. Assumptions: Commercial buyers' purchase decisions rest on measurable operating savings rather than brand or design alone; Home kitchens offer insufficient usage volume to repay a professional-grade unit's price; Professional service and installation networks cannot be replicated cheaply for consumers; Consumer demand for steam cooking is satisfied by cheaper countertop products. Predictions: Professional buyers cite time, labour and yield savings as main purchase reasons in surveys or case studies; Home buyers' willingness to pay falls sharply once the product is priced against cheaper countertop combi ovens; Consumer sales of a scaled-down unit do not reach the margin needed to justify separate product and channel costs.

T1 supports, from rational-anova-oven (market_fact): "Subsequent products included the Anova Precision Cooker Nano and the Anova Precision Oven, a countertop combi oven that supported both steam and convection cooking methods and could be used either alongside other Precision Cooker products or by itself.". Does not show: Whether home buyers will pay a premium over mainstream units, whether RATIONAL's brand or professional credibility transfers to home buyers, or what volume or margin a RATIONAL home product would achieve. It shows only that a consumer countertop combi oven exists in one market..

T2 supports, from rational-wiki-icombi90 (market_fact): "Combi ovens (iCombi product line) generate approximately 90% of Rational's appliance sales, while about 10% comes from the iVario series and newly added iHexagon appliances.". Does not show: Why commercial buyers purchase, whether labour or yield savings drive that choice, or whether home buyers would see the same economics. It shows the product mix is concentrated in combi ovens, not the cause of demand. The source is Wikipedia, a secondary summary, and its date is unknown..

Looked for evidence against T2: "home consumer demand for professional combi steamer premium countertop steam oven willingness to pay"; found rational-anova-oven, rational-combi-countertop, rational-combi-household.

T2 contradicts, from rational-combi-household (market_fact): "In addition to the professional food-service models, there are also smaller combi steamers for private household use.". Does not show: That households buy these units in volume, that they pay a margin-covering price, or that RATIONAL itself sells such a product. It also does not say which maker or model, or when. It weakens T2's assumption that no home market exists, but not T2's claim that professional value is larger..

Test "Premium home pre-order and price-response test" between T1; T2. Method: Landing page with a concept spec for a scaled-down professional steam combi for home kitchens, shown at three price points (randomised across visitors). Visitors who want it can place a refundable deposit. Paid search and targeted social ads to enthusiast home-cook audiences, plus a 20-person structured interview round with home cooks who already own a countertop steam or combi oven. Separately, a 10-call check with professional kitchen buyers to see whether they would buy a home version for their own use.. Sample: Proposed: about 2,000 unique visitors across the three price arms, and 20 interviews. Estimated: enough to detect a deposit rate difference of several percentage points.. Measure: Deposit conversion rate by price arm; share of interviewees who name a specific price they would pay and a reason tied to cooking outcome versus cost or space; share of professional buyers who express interest in a home version.. Predictions: T1: Deposit conversion at the premium arm stays at or above the threshold, and interviewees name steam-specific outcomes and accept a price several times that of mainstream countertop ovens.; T2: Deposit conversion falls sharply at the premium arm, interviewees cite space, cost or no need for professional-grade performance at home, and professional buyers show little interest in a home version.. Decision rule: Proposed: continue to a product-cost study only if the premium-arm deposit rate is at least 2% of visitors and at least 8 of 20 interviewees name a price at or above the premium arm with a steam-specific reason. Otherwise stop the home proposition and keep the professional focus. Treat results below 100 deposits as inconclusive and do not decide.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T2: Keep the professional-kitchen focus as the base case. Do not commit to a home-cook product yet. Run the low-cost premium pre-order and interview test (X1) before any product engineering. Proceed only if the decision rule is met. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: likely.

T1 kept: The simulated coordination result is not real data and does not bear on willingness to pay a premium, which is what T1 depends on, so it changes nothing. T1 stays open with the same assumptions and the same predictions for test X1. Its only real support remains the existence of a consumer countertop combi oven, which is a market fact, not proof of premium demand. New claim: none. Evidence: rational-anova-oven.

T2 kept: Treating SYN-RATIONAL-UPDATE as a what-if only: if it were real, it would show that installation coordination changes reservations among recruited home cooks, which is a friction effect that fits T2's view that home adoption depends on practical barriers. It does not show that home demand reaches margin, that professional value is smaller, or that RATIONAL needs new hardware. T2 is kept, and the result changes nothing in my recommendation. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-RATIONAL-UPDATE.

Recommendation: Stay with the professional-kitchen focus as the base case. Do not commit to a home-cook product or new hardware yet. Test the premium home-cook proposition cheaply first (X1), and proceed to product engineering only if its decision rule is met. Target customer: Professional kitchen operators (restaurants, canteens, hospitals, hotels and similar), which is the core of the current business. Home cooks remain a possible later segment, tested only through X1.. Value proposition: Professional combi-steamer systems that save labour, time and food waste across many meals a day. No home-cook value proposition is established yet.. Favoured theory: T2. Next action: Run test X1 (proposed, about EUR 18,000 and 10 weeks, both figures analyst estimates): a randomised premium pre-order and price-response test with enthusiast home cooks, 20 interviews, and 10 professional-buyer calls. Continue only if the premium-arm deposit rate is at least 2% and at least 8 of 20 interviewees name a price at or above the premium arm with a steam-specific reason.. Uncertainty: Several things are unresolved. I found no public evidence that RATIONAL itself sells to individual home buyers; the company's investor page lists professional customers only, and that is a company claim. My Wikipedia sources are secondary with unknown dates. I did not read any RATIONAL financial filings, so I cannot reconcile margins, the appliance split by segment, or home-market size. The Anova countertop combi oven and household combi steamers show that a home category exists, not that buyers will pay a premium for a RATIONAL product. The test budget and timeline are my assumptions.. Would change if: X1 meets its decision rule: the premium-arm deposit rate reaches at least 2% and at least 8 of 20 interviewees name a steam-specific reason at or above the premium price; Credible public data shows RATIONAL already sells to home buyers at a margin, or reports home-market revenue; Filings or market data show the home-cook category growing fast at premium prices, with reliable sizing; Professional-buyer calls show strong interest in a home version for their own use; A licensing or component partner offers to carry the home brand and cost, removing the need for RATIONAL's own channel. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: likely.

case.source_limits: Evidence is limited to the case dossier: each source shows everything the dossier holds for it, often a short excerpt, not the whole original. Results marked simulated are what-if evidence, not real observations.

The customer base ranges from restaurants and hotels, company canteens, hospitals, schools, universities, the military, prisons and retirement homes to fast-food restaurants, party services, supermarkets, bakeries and snack bars, butchers, petrol stations and delivery services, including so-called ghost kitchens.
According to company estimates, the global market potential for combi-steamers is 4.8 million customers, around 75% of whom still use traditional cooking appliances.

events.text: Objective: Decide whether RATIONAL AG should develop a differentiated proposition for home cooks using its commercial combi-steamer technology, or keep its focus on professional kitchens, and identify what evidence would justify each choice. The test is whether a home offering would earn a return that justifies the diversion from core commercial growth and brand risk.. Constraints: Outside analyst working only from public sources; no company contact or access to internal data; RATIONAL has not asked this question and nothing here describes its intentions; Partly public financials: note what cannot be found or reconciled; Test budget 20000 EUR and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions, not company figures; Seven searches remain; spend them carefully; Must first establish how far RATIONAL already sells to individual buyers rather than assume. Alternatives: A. No expansion: stay with professional kitchens and optimise the commercial core (service, financing, hospitality and institutional channels); B. Consumer-grade combi-steamer sold directly to home cooks under the RATIONAL brand, with a redesigned smaller unit; C. Licensing or co-branding the commercial technology to an established household appliance maker, which owns retail, marketing and home service; D. Prosumer line for serious home cooks sold through specialist retail, with a smaller price gap to commercial models; E. Channel-led entry: sell through existing dealers or kitchen-design partners to affluent renovation customers, without a separate consumer product; F. Bridge via small food-service operators (cafés, caterers, catering schools) before any home product, or software and cooking-data services around existing commercial units.
Searched for "RATIONAL combi steamer home cooking consumer sales"; found rational-ir-potential, rational-wiki-icombi90, rational-combi-makers.
Searched for "RATIONAL home cooking appliance households private customers"; found rational-ir-potential, rational-ir-customers, rational-combi-history.

T1: Affluent home cooks buy professional-grade cooking equipment as a status and performance signal. A compact, clearly commercial-derived unit sold directly to them would command a price premium that a home-appliance maker without a professional reputation cannot match. Who benefits: Affluent serious home cooks, who gain perceived performance and status; RATIONAL, which captures premium margin on a brand already associated with professional kitchens.. Why behaviour changes: Buyers who already spend heavily on pro-style ranges and cookware treat the professional brand as evidence of quality, so they will pay more for it than for an equivalent consumer appliance.. How value is captured: Direct or specialist-retail sales of a smaller, higher-priced unit, with margin protected by the brand rather than by commercial service contracts.. Assumptions: A meaningful segment of home buyers already pays premium prices for pro-style kitchen appliances; The commercial brand carries recognition among these buyers; A smaller unit can be built at a cost that still allows premium pricing; Home buyers will accept the footprint and power requirements. Predictions: Stated willingness to pay for a pro-branded home unit exceeds that for an otherwise identical unit with a consumer brand; Purchase intent concentrates in households that already own pro-style ranges or cookware; Conversion falls sharply if the price gap to consumer models is large relative to perceived brand benefit.

T2: Home cooks rarely use a combi-steamer after buying it because the value depends on knowing what to cook and how, not on the hardware. The hardware earns little repeat value on its own, so the durable revenue sits in guided recipes and cooking-program content, which a manufacturer with existing commercial program libraries can license. Who benefits: Home cooks who want to use the appliance regularly; RATIONAL, which could earn recurring revenue from recipe and program content rather than one-off hardware sales.. Why behaviour changes: Owners who receive tested programs for everyday dishes keep using the appliance, while owners left with only the manual abandon it after the first few uses.. How value is captured: Subscription or per-program fees for cooking content, or bundled content sold with the existing commercial hardware, rather than a new home unit.. Assumptions: Home owners underuse ovens and steamers without guided programs; Owners will pay recurring fees for programs they cannot easily build themselves; Commercial program libraries can be adapted to domestic dishes and portion sizes; The hardware installed base in homes is large enough to sell content to. Predictions: Households given guided programs use the appliance more often over eight weeks than households given only a manual; Willingness to pay for a program subscription is positive in owners but low in non-owners; Usage drop-off after month two is steeper without guided content.

T1 neutral, from rational-combi-makers (market_fact): "Germany: RATIONAL AG , Gaggenau Hausgeräte , PALUX, Convotherm, MKN, ELOMA, Miele , AEG (part of Electrolux), Bosch.". Does not show: Shows that home-appliance makers (Gaggenau, Miele, AEG, Bosch) already list combi-steamers in Germany, so the home segment has competition. It does not show whether home buyers pay a premium for a professional brand, what prices are charged, or whether RATIONAL sells any product to households..

T2 neutral, from rational-ir-customers (company_assertion): "The customer base ranges from restaurants and hotels, company canteens, hospitals, schools, universities, the military, prisons and retirement homes to fast-food restaurants, party services, supermarkets, bakeries and snack bars, butchers, petrol stations and delivery services, including so-called ghost kitchens.". Does not show: This is the company's own description of its customers. It lists only commercial and institutional buyers and says nothing about household use, usage frequency, or whether owners need recipe content to keep using a unit. It cannot test T2..

Looked for evidence against T1: "consumer willingness to pay premium professional brand home appliance versus consumer brand"; found rational-anova-electrolux, rational-combi-household, rational-focus-quote.

T1 neutral, from rational-combi-household (market_fact): "In addition to the professional food-service models, there are also smaller combi steamers for private household use.". Does not show: Confirms that smaller household combi-steamers exist, which makes the home segment real. It does not show that buyers pay more for a professional brand, what price premium exists, or whether RATIONAL sells to households. The challenge found no evidence against T1 yet, and this source does not contradict it..

Test "Price-gap and guided-use concept test for a pro-branded compact unit" between T1; T2. Method: Online conjoint and stated-preference survey of German households that already own a premium oven or range, with two arms: (a) same compact unit shown with the RATIONAL brand versus a consumer brand, at the same price; (b) unit shown with versus without a guided-program subscription, priced at a proposed monthly fee. Followed by a 4-week diary sub-sample of 60 households receiving a loaned unit with guided programs versus manual only.. Sample: Proposed: about 600 online respondents screened for premium cooking appliance ownership, plus 60 diary households (30 per arm). Estimated panel cost within budget.. Measure: Stated willingness to pay (brand arm), purchase intent, and subscription take-up (program arm); weekly self-reported and logged use of the unit in the diary sub-sample.. Predictions: T1: Pro brand raises stated willingness to pay by a clear margin over the consumer brand at equal price; the uplift concentrates in owners of pro-style ranges and cookware.; T2: Brand uplift is small or absent; the diary arm with guided programs shows materially higher weekly use and subscription take-up than manual-only.. Decision rule: Pursue a brand-led compact product (T1) only if the pro-brand arm shows at least a 15% higher stated willingness to pay than the consumer-brand arm, with the effect concentrated in pro-appliance owners. Pursue a content-led model (T2) only if guided-program households use the unit at least 50% more often weekly and at least 25% of them take up a subscription at the proposed fee. If neither threshold is met, do not expand into home cooks. The 15% and 50% thresholds and 25% take-up are proposed analyst thresholds, not observed values.. Cost: 18500 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not commit to a home-cook product yet. Keep the professional focus as the base case. Run the proposed X1 concept test before any build decision. T1 is the only theory with a direct route to a brand-led compact unit, so it is the one to test first, but neither theory has evidence in its favour yet. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Stay with professional kitchens as the base case. Do not commit to a home-cook product now. Run the proposed X1 concept test (about EUR 18,500, 10 weeks, proposed figures) before any build decision. Target customer: No home-cook target yet. If X1 supports it, the first candidates are affluent households that already own premium or pro-style ranges and cookware.. Value proposition: Untested. A compact unit carrying the professional brand (T1), or guided-program content (T2). Neither is supported by evidence yet.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the X1 test with a panel or partner, collecting the brand-versus-consumer willingness-to-pay arm and the guided-program diary arm, then apply the decision rule.. Uncertainty: High. Public sources show RATIONAL's customers are commercial and institutional, and home combi-steamers exist from other makers. I found no source showing RATIONAL sells to households, no pricing or margin data for a home unit, and no evidence that home buyers pay a premium for a professional brand. The company's 4.8 million potential-customer claim is unverified. Thresholds are my proposals.. Would change if: X1 shows at least 15% higher stated willingness to pay for the pro-branded arm, concentrated in pro-appliance owners; Guided-program households use the unit at least 50% more often and at least 25% take up a subscription; Independent data showing a large, growing household segment with proven premium pricing; Evidence that RATIONAL already sells to households, changing the baseline; Evidence that home buyers do not pay for a professional brand, shifting the question toward content or channel options. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

case.question: Should Aquaporin A/S develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing water-membrane offering? What evidence would justify that investment?
case.source_limits: Evidence is limited to the case dossier: each source shows everything the dossier holds for it, often a short excerpt, not the whole original. Results marked simulated are what-if evidence, not real observations.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 households already using a compatible drinking-water purifier received the same membrane specifications, water-quality information, brand, warranty and total annual price. Half were offered a prepaid plan with scheduled cartridge delivery and replacement reminders; half were offered a prepaid self-service cartridge plan without that delivery schedule or reminders. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid plan enrollment remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned households per arm. This what-if assumes an authorised operator can legally supply and service the offer; it does not change the dossier evidence about Aquaporin's insolvency or financing. There were 120 plan enrollments in the scheduled-delivery-and-reminder plan arm and 60 in the self-service cartridge plan arm. This tests willingness to enroll in a maintenance offer under that conditional supply assumption, not membrane efficacy, correct long-term filter use, market size, company solvency or Aquaporin's ability to fund an offer. An unchanged business recommendation can be justified by those other constraints.

The decrease was mainly driven by an unexpected change in demand from Aquaporin's largest key account in Drinking Water and a change in timing of a Forward Osmosis project. In Industrial Water, revenue increased significantly by 192% to DKK 10.5 million, while Drinking Water decreased by 55% to DKK 18 million and Forward Osmosis Market Development decreased by 27% to DKK 12 million.

With only two cartridges and a replacement indicator on the machine, ONE is easy to install and use. The user friendliness continues, as ONE’s only maintenance requirement is cartridge replacement which can easily be done by oneself.

Signed an exclusive supply agreement with AquaShield, the global brand partner of Philips Water Solutions for supply of membrane to all Philips-branded purifiers in China, with a doubling of sales compared to 2022

Despite significant efforts through a period of time and as part of its strategic review in the second half of 2025, where multiple routes have been explored with the view to raise capital, enter into a strategic transaction, or a sale of part of or all of the Company's asset, the Company has not been successful in identifying investors or partners that can provide sufficient funding to continue the Company's commercialization and advancing its proprietary water technology platform. The Board of Directors does therefore not see a viable path forward to secure a sustainable financing solution as a going concern.

events.text: Objective: Decide whether Aquaporin A/S should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing water-membrane offering, and identify what evidence would justify that investment. Outside view using public sources only.. Constraints: Outside view only; no company contact or stated intentions; Test budget 20000 EUR and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions, not company figures; Financial data may be incomplete; flag gaps; Find out existing reach to individual buyers rather than assume it; Only 7 searches remain; Company claims are not proof of demand. Alternatives: No expansion: keep selling membranes B2B/OEM only; Product redesign: finished consumer purifier on existing membrane tech, sold direct; Different route to buyers: license membrane to existing purifier brands as ingredient branding; Different customer group: institutional or emergency/off-grid buyers instead of households; Narrow use-case pilot: one niche such as travel, camping or emergency preparedness, tested before wider commitment; Partner-led consumer launch: co-branded product with an appliance or retail partner sharing risk.
Searched for "Aquaporin consumer water purifier"; found aqp-one-purifier-2021, aqp-philips-china-supply-2023, aqp-vestel-rafine-pro-2024.

T1: Aquaporin captures more value by licensing its membrane as an ingredient inside partner-branded purifiers than by selling its own consumer brand, because partners already own the shelf, service and brand trust that consumers use to choose a purifier. Who benefits: Aquaporin (membrane margin without brand and channel costs) and partner appliance brands such as Vestel and the Philips-branded China partner, which get a differentiated technology claim.. Why behaviour changes: Households buy a water purifier from a brand and retailer they already trust. A visible ingredient claim ('Aquaporin Inside') adds a technology reason to buy without the buyer needing to trust a new unknown brand.. How value is captured: Per-unit membrane supply or licence fees paid by the partner, plus exclusivity fees. Aquaporin's revenue scales with partner unit volume rather than with its own consumer marketing spend.. Assumptions: Partner brands pay for the technology claim, so the membrane premium is real and not just a supply commodity; Consumers respond to an ingredient badge at point of sale; Aquaporin does not need to carry warranty and service risk for the consumer product; Partner volumes, not Aquaporin's own brand, drive future revenue. Predictions: Partner-branded products with the ingredient badge sell at a higher retail price or margin than equivalent unbadged products in the same market; Aquaporin's revenue growth tracks partner unit sales, not its own marketing spend; Exclusivity or minimum-volume clauses appear in supply agreements; Own-brand ONE sales stay small relative to partner-channel supply.

T2: In a specific use case where buyers care about verifiable performance rather than brand familiarity, an Aquaporin-controlled own brand can earn a premium margin that partner-branded products cannot, because the membrane's performance becomes the main purchase reason and the manufacturer keeps the full retail margin. Who benefits: Aquaporin, which would capture retail margin and customer data, and buyers in the niche who get a performance guarantee they cannot check in ordinary purifiers.. Why behaviour changes: Buyers in travel, emergency or off-grid use value a specific, checkable claim (for example removal of named contaminants per certified test) more than a familiar brand name. The technology is the reason to buy, so the brand that owns the claim gets the sale.. How value is captured: Direct sales margin on the finished product and cartridge refills, which are a recurring cartridge-replacement revenue stream. Aquaporin keeps the consumer relationship and can price the performance claim.. Assumptions: A niche exists that is large enough and will pay a premium for verifiable performance; The claim can be certified or independently tested, so it is credible; Aquaporin can absorb marketing, service and warranty costs for a consumer brand; Partner-branded products do not already capture this niche. Predictions: Buyers in the niche show higher willingness to pay for a certified performance claim than for an unlabelled product, in a conjoint or price test; Cartridge refill purchase rates are high enough to support a recurring-revenue model; Own-brand direct sales need a customer-acquisition cost below the expected margin over the product life; Partner-branded sales in the same niche stay low, which would show the gap is real.

T1 supports, from aqp-vestel-rafine-pro-2024 (company_assertion): "The Aquaporin Inside® technology powers the Vestel Rafine PRO water purifier.". Does not show: Does not show that the ingredient badge raised price, margin or sales, that consumers chose the product for the membrane, or the volume Vestel sells. It is a launch announcement from Aquaporin, not independent data..

T2 neutral, from aqp-one-purifier-2021 (company_assertion): "With only two cartridges and a replacement indicator on the machine, ONE is easy to install and use.". Does not show: Does not show a performance premium, a price, a margin, a verified contaminant claim or any buyer who paid for performance. The ONE is sold through distributors in several regions, so it does not show that Aquaporin keeps the full retail margin. The source is a product launch claim..

Looked for evidence against T1: "Aquaporin membrane licence supply margin partner brand revenue dependence risk"; found aqp-philips-china-supply-2023, aqp-strategic-review-failed, aqp-fy2024-drinking-water-drop.

Declined to test: Aquaporin announced on 30 January 2026 that it had withdrawn its offering, could not find investors or partners to fund commercialization, and would initiate insolvency proceedings. A consumer test would need a company that can fund and run it, and its partner and own-brand routes lack that funding. The proposed 20000 EUR and 12-week test would not change the decision, because the company cannot take on a new consumer investment whatever the test shows. Additional demand evidence would not be decisive here, so testing is not worth its cost.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a new differentiated consumer proposition now. The company has announced withdrawal of its offering and insolvency proceedings (30 January 2026), so it cannot fund one. Any future move should be a licence or ingredient-brand arrangement that a funded third party pays for, not an Aquaporin-owned consumer launch. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: The result is simulated, so it is a what-if and not evidence. If it were real, it would bear on whether households enrol in a prepaid cartridge-maintenance plan, which is a consumer-channel question. It would not bear on the licence or ingredient-brand mechanism that T1 describes, and it says nothing about Aquaporin's solvency or ability to fund an offer. The stated scope excludes those points. T1 stays as it was, with the partner-dependence and funding limits already recorded. The result changes nothing in the recommendation. New claim: none. Evidence: aqp-strategic-review-failed.

T2 kept: The simulated result is a what-if, so it is not cited as evidence. If it were real, it would show only that households might enrol in a prepaid cartridge-maintenance plan under a conditional supply assumption, which bears on a consumer service rather than on the performance premium that T2 claims. It does not show a premium, a price, or that Aquaporin can fund or run an own-brand offer. T2 is kept as uncertain. Its own-brand premium is still untested, and the company's insolvency means it cannot currently be pursued by Aquaporin. New claim: none. Evidence: aqp-one-purifier-2021.

T1 kept: Hypothetical only: SYN-AQP-UPDATE is a simulated result, not real data. If it were real, it would show that a prepaid maintenance plan with scheduled delivery and reminders gets more enrolments than a self-service plan. That is a consumer-channel result for an authorised operator, and it would not show that partner licensing captures value, nor that Aquaporin can fund or run such an offer. T1 is kept. The insolvency evidence still governs the recommendation, and the result does not change it. It is excluded from the finish evidence. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-AQP-UPDATE; aqp-strategic-review-failed.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case now. Aquaporin announced on 30 January 2026 that it had withdrawn its offering and would initiate insolvency proceedings, after failing to find investors or partners to fund commercialization. The real question is whether the company can fund any new investment, and on public evidence it cannot. If a funded third party wants to take the membrane into a consumer product, the right structure is a licence or ingredient-brand arrangement in which that party carries the brand, channel and working capital. Target customer: None for Aquaporin at present. Households already reached through partner-branded purifiers, such as the Vestel Rafine PRO in Turkey and Philips-branded purifiers in China, are served by partners, not by an Aquaporin consumer proposition.. Value proposition: Membrane technology supplied as an ingredient inside partner-branded purifiers, with exclusivity or volume terms. Not an Aquaporin-owned consumer brand while the company lacks funding.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Treat the company as a going-concern risk, not a growth investment. If the question stays open, check the insolvency outcome, whether a buyer or licensee takes over the membrane platform, and whether partner supply agreements such as the China exclusivity survive. Do not commission the 20000 EUR consumer test until a funded owner exists.. Uncertainty: I did not read the company's financial statements, so there are no absolute revenue, cash or debt figures. The 95% growth and China doubling are company claims with no base. No independent data on demand, price premiums or replacement rates was found. The ONE distributor list is from a 2021 press release. The insolvency notice is a third-party copy; its outcome is unknown. The simulated result was not used as evidence.. Would change if: Insolvency ends with a buyer or investor who keeps the membrane platform and funds consumer or licensed products; Independent evidence shows badged purifiers sell at a price premium over unbadged ones; Audited accounts show enough cash for a funded consumer launch; A funded partner offers a licence or co-branded launch carrying the brand, channel and working capital; Independent research shows a niche such as travel or emergency pays a premium for certified performance. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 households already using a compatible drinking-water purifier received the same membrane specifications, water-quality information, brand, warranty and total annual price. Half were offered a prepaid plan with scheduled cartridge delivery and replacement reminders; half were offered a prepaid self-service cartridge plan without that delivery schedule or reminders. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid plan enrollment remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned households per arm. This what-if assumes an authorised operator can legally supply and service the offer; it does not change the dossier evidence about Aquaporin's insolvency or financing. There were 120 plan enrollments in the scheduled-delivery-and-reminder plan arm and 60 in the self-service cartridge plan arm. This tests willingness to enroll in a maintenance offer under that conditional supply assumption, not membrane efficacy, correct long-term filter use, market size, company solvency or Aquaporin's ability to fund an offer. An unchanged business recommendation can be justified by those other constraints.

events.text: Objective: Decide whether Aquaporin A/S should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for one specific use case, beyond its existing membrane offering, and identify the evidence that would justify that investment.. Constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only; no contact with the company; Company intentions unknown; financial data may be incomplete and gaps must be stated; Test budget EUR 20000 and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions; Search budget is limited; only observed facts from read sources may be presented as observed. Alternatives: No expansion: remain a B2B membrane supplier with the current offering; Product redesign: a consumer drinking-water purifier or pitcher using existing membranes, sold through current channels; Different route to buyers: license or OEM supply to established household water-filter brands; Different customer group: compact point-of-use units for cafes, offices, hotels or schools; Different use case: niche such as travel, emergency or off-grid purification; Adjacent-market pivot: biomimetic membranes for non-drinking uses such as food concentration or pharmaceuticals.
Searched for "Aquaporin consumer water purifier"; found aqp-one-purifier-2021, aqp-philips-china-supply-2023, aqp-vestel-rafine-pro-2024.

T1: Consumers choose drinking-water purifiers on brand, design and retail reach, not on the membrane inside. Aquaporin captures value best as an ingredient supplier that brand partners sell under their own names, so a direct consumer product adds little. Who benefits: Brand partners such as Philips (via AquaShield in China) and Vestel (Rafine PRO in Turkey) gain a differentiated membrane claim and own the consumer relationship. Aquaporin gains exclusive supply volume.. Why behaviour changes: Partners' marketing, retail shelf and trusted brand name persuade buyers. The membrane technology acts as a supporting credential that the partner can advertise without the buyer needing to understand it.. How value is captured: Exclusive or long-term supply agreements priced per membrane or per unit sold, possibly with licence fees, rather than selling to end users.. Assumptions: Partners see the Aquaporin Inside claim as a reason to buy; Exclusivity holds and partner volumes are large enough to matter; Consumers do not pay a separate premium that Aquaporin could capture directly. Predictions: Partner-branded product sales rise after Aquaporin-branded launches and are reported as Aquaporin revenue growth; Aquaporin revenue concentrates in a few partner agreements; Direct-to-consumer sales by Aquaporin remain small or absent in public reports.

T2: Households buy a purifier mainly for the replacement cartridge economics and convenience. A maker that owns the cartridge format and its supply can earn recurring revenue, so the membrane's performance matters less than the consumable lock-in. Who benefits: A consumer-facing maker that controls the cartridge; households gain lower cost per litre only if cartridges are priced below rivals.. Why behaviour changes: Buyers judge a purifier by running cost and how easy cartridge replacement is, which the device sales price does not show. A recurring-cost story can shift choice toward the brand with the cheaper or more convenient cartridge.. How value is captured: Margin on repeat cartridge sales over the device lifetime, not on the one-off device sale.. Assumptions: Cartridge cost is a large share of lifetime cost for buyers; Buyers compare cartridge prices across brands; Cartridges can be made proprietary or hard to substitute. Predictions: Buyers who pay attention to running cost choose the lower-cartridge-cost brand; Cartridge revenue becomes a larger share of total revenue than device sales for a consumer product; Products with proprietary cartridges show higher repeat purchase rates than open-format ones.

T1 supports, from aqp-philips-china-supply-2023 (company_assertion): "Signed an exclusive supply agreement with AquaShield, the global brand partner of Philips Water Solutions for supply of membrane to all Philips-branded purifiers in China, with a doubling of sales compared to 2022". Does not show: Why Chinese buyers chose Philips purifiers, whether the membrane claim drove that choice, or whether the doubling of sales came from membrane volume or from Philips' own sales. Also it is a company's own bullet point, not audited figures..

T2 neutral, from aqp-one-purifier-2021 (company_assertion): "ONE’s only maintenance requirement is cartridge replacement which can easily be done by oneself.". Does not show: Cartridge price, how often buyers replace cartridges, whether cartridges are proprietary, or whether buyers compare running costs. It only shows that the product's maintenance is cartridge replacement, which is a feature claim, not evidence of purchase behaviour..
Looked for evidence against T1: "Aquaporin direct consumer sales membrane brand choice"; found aqp-philips-china-supply-2023, aqp-strategic-review-failed, aqp-dwd-recital40-confidence.

T1 contradicts, from aqp-strategic-review-failed (company_assertion): "the Company has not been successful in identifying investors or partners that can provide sufficient funding to continue the Company's commercialization and advancing its proprietary water technology platform". Does not show: Why partners did not fund the company: whether partner royalties were too small, whether the membrane claim lacked buyer value, or whether the cause was investor appetite or cost. It also does not show partner volumes or revenue split, so it cannot rule out T1 on its own. It does show the partner-supply route did not produce enough value to fund the company..

Declined to test: The company announced on 30 January 2026 that it has withdrawn its offering and resolved to initiate insolvency proceedings, after failing to find investors or partners to fund commercialisation. A EUR 20,000, 12-week consumer test would not address the binding constraint, which is whether any funded route to market exists at all. Any consumer or partner proposition would need capital the company has been unable to raise, so a test cannot justify investment in this company. The result would not change the decision not to invest.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for Aquaporin A/S. The company has announced withdrawal of its offering and the start of insolvency proceedings (announcement No. 04/2026, 30 January 2026). Its partner-supply route, the one theory with some company-reported support, did not raise enough capital to continue. Any consumer proposition would first need a funded route to market, which the company has not shown it can obtain. Anyone still considering the question should check the current insolvency status and the terms of the Philips and Vestel supply arrangements, which I could not find. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: unlikely.

T2 kept: No observed evidence supports T2 yet. The only source bearing on it, aqp-one-purifier-2021, says only that cartridge replacement is the maintenance task, which is a feature claim. I have not counted the SIMULATED update, since it is not real. As a what-if it would suggest convenience, not membrane performance, drives plan enrolment, but it does not test cartridge price or running cost, and it leaves open whether Aquaporin can fund an offer. New claim: none. Evidence: aqp-one-purifier-2021.

T1 revised: The insolvency announcement (aqp-strategic-review-failed) states the company could not find investors or partners to fund commercialisation. That contradicts the prediction that partner supply volumes would sustain the company. T1 still explains the reported partner deals, but it does not explain their failure to fund the company, so I narrow the claim to the consumer-facing brand side. New claim: Partners own the consumer relationship and the brand. The membrane supplier earns only if partner volume is large enough to fund its own operations, which the evidence does not show.. Evidence: aqp-strategic-review-failed; aqp-philips-china-supply-2023.

T2 kept: Kept at prior status. The only real source bearing on T2, aqp-one-purifier-2021, describes cartridge replacement as a maintenance task, not buyer choice or running cost. The SIMULATED update is not counted as evidence. New claim: none. Evidence: aqp-one-purifier-2021. (made 2 times in a row)
The investigation stopped before a recommendation (repeated errors).
