events.text: Objective: Decide whether Aquaporin A/S should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its existing water-membrane business, and identify what evidence would justify that investment rather than assuming consumer demand.. Constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only; the company has not asked and nothing here describes its intentions; Financial data may be incomplete; state what could not be found; Test budget of 20000 EUR and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions, not company figures; Search budget is 7 searches remaining; use each one deliberately; Company's own claims are not proof of consumer demand; No SIMULATED results may be cited in finish. Alternatives: A. No expansion: remain a B2B or OEM membrane supplier and invest nothing in consumer products; B. Product redesign: develop a consumer-grade household purifier cartridge or module sold through existing OEM partners; C. Different route to buyers: direct-to-consumer brand or subscription for replacement membranes; D. Different customer group: target institutional, emergency or off-grid water buyers such as hospitality, disaster relief or remote housing, rather than mainstream households; E. Licensing or white-label: license the membrane technology to appliance makers who own the consumer relationship; F. Staged option: a low-cost validation test such as concept testing or pre-orders before any build decision.
Searched for "Aquaporin consumer water filter household product"; found aqp-srilanka-filter-disuse, aqp-dwd-recital40-confidence, aqp-eurostat-household-use.

T1: Households in water-secure countries buy point-of-use filters mainly to reduce distrust of tap water, so a filter that visibly proves its performance could earn a recurring replacement-membrane revenue stream from a trust-driven segment. Who benefits: Households that doubt tap taste or safety, and a manufacturer that sells replacement membranes on a recurring basis. Why behaviour changes: A verifiable, visible performance signal (e.g. certification or an indicator) reduces doubt about tap water and turns a vague worry into a purchase that feels justified. How value is captured: Aquaporin owns the membrane and its replacement cycle, or licenses the membrane to a brand that sells the cartridge, earning a margin on each replacement. Assumptions: A meaningful share of households in target markets already drink mostly tap water but report taste or safety doubts; Trust, not price or convenience, is the main reason to buy; Households will keep paying for replacement cartridges once they own the unit. Predictions: Purchase intent rises more when the product shows a measured performance result than when it shows only a design or convenience claim; Households with higher self-reported tap-water distrust show higher willingness to pay for a verifiable filter; Repeat replacement purchase after the first cartridge is measurable in a 12-week pilot.

T2: Filters bought for households in water-secure countries are abandoned because they break, need upkeep, or stop being used, so the value is held by whoever controls the unit's durability and service rather than by the filter's performance; a manufacturer that sells to institutions or emergency buyers, who buy for function and maintain the units, captures value more reliably than one selling to mainstream households. Who benefits: Institutional or emergency buyers (NGOs, hospitality, relief agencies) who need reliable units and will pay for service, and the manufacturer who supplies membranes and service contracts to them. Why behaviour changes: Buyers who depend on the water for function judge the product on uptime and maintenance, not on a feeling of trust, so they keep units in use and reorder when the service is reliable. How value is captured: Aquaporin supplies membranes and service or replacement contracts to institutional buyers, earning recurring revenue tied to uptime rather than to consumer enthusiasm. Assumptions: Institutional buyers have a recurring, funded need for water purification; Consumer abandonment is driven mainly by breakage and upkeep rather than by a lack of perceived need; Institutional buyers will sign service or replacement agreements. Predictions: Units placed with a service agreement stay in use longer than units sold without one; Breakage and maintenance failure, not stated lack of interest, are the leading causes of disuse in institutional deployments; Institutional buyers reorder membranes at a higher and steadier rate than mainstream household buyers.

T1 neutral, from aqp-dwd-recital40-confidence (regulation): "The purpose of better consumer knowledge of relevant information and improved transparency should be to increase citizens' confidence in the water supplied to them". Does not show: This is the EU's stated policy aim. It does not show how many households distrust tap water, whether distrust drives filter purchases, or whether a filter would address it..

T2 supports, from aqp-srilanka-filter-disuse (independent_study): "At the time of survey, 24% of households (107/452) did not use filters; the most common reason given was breakage (42%).". Does not show: The study covers ceramic filters distributed after the 2004 tsunami in Sri Lanka, not household purchases in water-secure countries or Aquaporin products. I only read the abstract, so I cannot confirm the other reasons for disuse or the study's method. It supports the claim that breakage drives disuse in one aid-distribution setting, not that institutional buyers would keep units in use..

Looked for evidence against T2: "ceramic water filter disuse reasons breakage not main cause institutional deployment abandonment"; found aqp-srilanka-filter-disuse, aqp-flint-filters-not-working, aqp-newark-filter-indicators.

T2 contradicts, from aqp-flint-filters-not-working (customer_observation): "“Anywhere from 50 to 70 percent of folks that we’re seeing have filters that are not working,”". Does not show: This is an official's estimate about a crisis setting, not a measured failure rate, and it does not say whether breakage was the cause. It may reflect misuse or neglect rather than breakage. It challenges my claim that breakage is the main driver of disuse, but it does not show that institutional buyers would lapse, and it is not a controlled study..

T1 neutral, from aqp-newark-filter-indicators (independent_study): "Many of the filters in the “less than one week” category are a result of the sampler providing a new filter cartridge to residents that had a red light indicator on their filter or no filter at all.". Does not show: This is a municipal sampling report about filter status and replacement. It shows that a visible indicator was linked to replacement in one sampling exercise, but it does not show that households distrust tap water or that a visible signal would raise purchase intent or willingness to pay..

Test "Trust versus service pilot: consumer and institutional arms" between T1; T2. Method: Proposed 12-week pilot with two arms. Arm A: households in a water-secure European city, randomly given either a filter with a visible performance indicator or a standard filter, at a discounted price. Arm B: a small set of hospitality or workplace sites given units with a service agreement or without one. Track use, breakage and replacement orders.. Sample: Proposed estimate: about 120 households (60 per consumer arm) and about 8 institutional sites (4 per arm). Sizes are analyst assumptions, not company figures.. Measure: Share of units still in use at week 12; breakage and maintenance-failure rate; reported tap-water distrust at baseline; replacement-cartridge reorder rate; stated willingness to pay for a verifiable indicator.. Predictions: T1: Households given the visible performance indicator show higher reported willingness to pay and higher reorder than standard-filter households, and baseline tap-water distrust predicts uptake.; T2: Institutional units with a service agreement stay in use longer than units without one, and breakage or upkeep, not stated lack of interest, is the main cause of disuse; the indicator arm shows no lift in reorder.. Decision rule: Proceed toward a consumer proposition only if the indicator arm shows at least 15 percentage points higher stated willingness to pay than standard, and baseline distrust predicts uptake. Otherwise favour the institutional or service route if service-agreement units show at least 20 percentage points higher use at week 12. If neither threshold is met, do not invest. Thresholds are proposed estimates.. Cost: 18000 euros, 12 weeks.

Favours T2: Do not build a consumer-facing differentiated proposition now. Stay with the B2B or OEM membrane business, and if pursuing a new use case, test an institutional or service-based route first (alternatives D and staged option F), because the evidence I have read is thin and mostly not about Aquaporin's products or about households in water-secure markets. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Do not commit to a differentiated consumer proposition now. Keep the existing B2B or OEM membrane business as the base. If pursuing a new use case, run the proposed low-cost test X1 on an institutional or service-based route before any consumer build. I found no evidence that Aquaporin sells to individual buyers, so its current consumer position remains unverified. Target customer: Not yet chosen. Leading candidate is institutional or emergency buyers needing reliable units with service. Untested hypothesis.. Value proposition: Reliable membrane performance with replacement and service contracts so units stay in use. Not yet validated with buyers.. Favoured theory: T2. Next action: Read Aquaporin's own product and annual-report disclosures to establish current consumer reach, since my search did not return them. Then run test X1 (proposed, about 18,000 EUR over 12 weeks, analyst estimates) before any build decision.. Uncertainty: High. Evidence is thin: the Sri Lanka study is an abstract on ceramic filters after a tsunami, not Aquaporin products; the Flint figure is an official's crisis estimate; Newark shows indicator-triggered replacement only; the EU recital is a policy aim; Eurostat gives water use, not filter purchases. No Aquaporin revenue or market data found. Both theories rated uncertain.. Would change if: Aquaporin's disclosures show existing individual-buyer sales with measurable repeat membrane revenue; Surveys show high tap-water distrust predicting willingness to pay for a verifiable filter (supports T1); Institutional deployments show breakage or upkeep as main disuse cause, with service keeping units in use (supports T2); Test X1 meets either decision threshold; Evidence that the cited disuse studies do not transfer to modern filters. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.
